title: What Makes You 'You': Exploring The Idea of Self

detail.title: What Makes You 'You': Exploring The Idea of Self
detail.abstract: This is an analytical paper that examines and draws inferences on what essentially constitutes the self. Consulting important ideas and theories from both classical and contemporary literature, the study also employs a survey with 255 participants to gather original empirical data to provide broader perspectives on the subject, based on which it attempts to conceptualise a diachronically stable 'I', associated with and yet different from an integrated self-concept. It concisely reviews insights from cognitive psychology, neuropsychology, social psychology, as well as other related disciplines, and incorporates these interdependent mechanisms into a unified theory. It finally concludes that the self is a temporal continuum of consciousness, sentience, and centre of attentional processes that manifests itself in a 'first person' narrative, distinct from the experience of other non-self entities.

title: Behavior-Based Pricing under Informed Privacy Consent: Unraveling Autonomy Paradox
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Twin Cities, Carlson School of Management, Students, University of Minnesota - Twin Cities and University of Minnesota - Twin Cities - Carlson School of Management

detail.title: Behavior-Based Pricing under Informed Privacy Consent: Unraveling Autonomy Paradox
detail.abstract: The implementation of recent privacy protection regulations mandates that firms obtain privacy consent from consumers before acquiring their private data. This procedure, known as "informed privacy consent," has significant implications for behavior-based pricing, wherein firms engage in third-degree price discrimination based on consumers' purchase history. Before keeping track of consumers' purchasing history for implementing price discrimination, firms must seek consumers' privacy consent, enabling consumers to autonomously make decisions regarding their data. These endogenous privacy decisions are shaped by several factors, such as the cost of risk from privacy breaches, anticipation of future utility changes driven by price discrimination and personalized products, or rewards for opting in. Although consumers strategically decide their privacy choices to get the best future utility, in equilibrium, none of them exclusively benefit from their choices, which leads to a decrease in overall consumer surplus even with the enhanced utility from personalized products and rewards for opting in. Firms, despite the cost of providing the rewards, earn higher profits by exploiting consumers' strategic privacy decisions, which alleviates price competition. Our findings underscore an autonomy paradox that empowering consumers to make informed decisions about their privacy rights does not necessarily lead to increased consumer surplus. This result implies privacy regulations founded on informed consent may lead to unintended consequences.

detail.abstract: Opaque (or probabilistic) products combine several traditional products into a menu of alternatives, with the specific product revealed only after purchase. Such offers are increasingly common across industries because they allow sellers to segment customers not only by price sensitivity but also by the strength of their preferences for specific components. Most existing research relies on Hotellingtype models that restrict opaque products to two components and impose a highly specific preference structure. This excludes settings in which (some) customers appreciate multiple components simultaneously, dislike all of them, or where opaque products consist of more than two components. We address these limitations by generalizing to a numerical framework that accommodates arbitrary customer preference distributions and an unrestricted number of component products. Prices and assignment probabilities are jointly optimized using a novel Branch-and-Cut algorithm, a Fix-and-Optimize heuristic, and a Genetic Algorithm. A numerical study shows that Branch-and-Cut outperforms a commercial solver, while the Genetic Algorithm delivers strong performance and is suitable for practical use.

title: Who You Notice Might Not be Who You Choose: Proximity as Collaboration Choice Architecture

detail.title: Who You Notice Might Not be Who You Choose: Proximity as Collaboration Choice Architecture
detail.abstract: Organizations invest heavily in spatial proximity to promote collaboration, yet proximity interventions yield inconsistent outcomes: some generate new cross-boundary ties, others concentrate collaboration among familiar partners, and still others reduce face-to-face interaction. Existing accounts emphasizing awareness, coordination convenience, and relational trust cannot adjudicate these patterns because they treat collaborator choice as a single revealed outcome and lack a mechanism through which visibility can suppress initiation. This article develops a theory of proximity as collaboration choice architecture, separating collaboration formation into three analytically distinct stages: consideration set formation, initiation, and partner selection. It specifies how spatial design features differentially affect each stage. Encounter generation and work legibility expand whom actors credibly consider; coordination-cost differentials and relational affordances shift heuristic weighting toward feasible or safe partners, concentrating realized collaboration; and control and interruptibility cues increase engagement frictions that can prevent exposure from converting into initiation. This staging yields two discriminating predictions: proximity can broaden consideration sets while narrowing realized partner portfolios, and design features that increase legibility can nonetheless reduce initiation, producing channel substitution away from face-to-face interaction. The framework reconciles mixed evidence, clarifies which outcomes diagnose which mechanisms, and offers a diagnostic vocabulary for designing collaborative work environments.

title: Subtractive Marketing Methodology: Eliminating Defense Triggers Instead of Strengthening Arguments
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Subtractive Marketing Methodology: Eliminating Defense Triggers Instead of Strengthening Arguments
detail.abstract: Professional marketing texts do not fail because of quality. They fail because a classification system in the receiver's mind categorizes incoming communication as a persuasion attempt and stops processing before conscious evaluation begins. The subtractive marketing methodology is a 6-stage cascade that eliminates defense triggers instead of strengthening arguments. It operates on the mechanism level of this classification system, which means it terminates through finite, testable constraints, a property that conventional approaches lack. This methodology was developed bottom-up from a single use case, N=1. It is explicitly falsifiable and names four testable conditions under which it would fail.

detail.abstract:
For five decades, competitive strategy has oriented businesses against each other — positioning firms against industry forces and competitors — while the customer remained a variable. This paper argues that orientation constitutes a structural misalignment between what businesses measure and what actually determines their survival.
The consequences are now acute. The customer has become informed, mobile, and equipped. Switching costs have collapsed. Power has migrated from the business to the customer. The tools built to address this — Customer Lifetime Value and churn modelling — measure consequence without interrogating cause. CLV asks what the customer is worth. The churn model detects when they are leaving. Neither asks the prior question: who has this customer become?
This paper introduces the Relationship Intelligence Value Framework — RIV-F — repositioning the customer relationship as the primary unit of strategic intelligence across four dimensions: Trajectory, Triggers, Shape, and Depth. It introduces the Semiotic Worker — the human cognitive role required to operationalise RIV-F — and the Living Organisation — the business that continuously evolves in response to the living reality of its customer relationships rather than positioning against external forces.
Grounded in the history of strategic thought and anchored in African banking and mobile money markets, this paper argues that the competitive edge of the next decade is not speed, not AI. It is alignment.

detail.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Transforming Modern Manufacturing Operations
detail.abstract: This study explores the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in modern manufacturing operations, focusing on how AI adoption reshapes production processes, workforce dynamics, supply chain management, and organizational performance. As manufacturing systems become increasingly complex and data-driven, AI provides the capacity to analyze large volumes of operational data, optimize production workflows, enhance quality control, and enable predictive maintenance. The research adopts a qualitative methodology based on an extensive review of recent academic and industry literature, identifying key themes and insights related to AI implementation in manufacturing contexts. Twelve major thematic areas emerged from the analysis, including intelligent production systems, predictive maintenance, quality control automation, supply chain integration, production planning optimization, workforce transformation, energy efficiency, sustainability practices, decision-support systems, innovation in product design, human-machine collaboration, and organizational agility. The study demonstrates that AI technologies facilitate autonomous and adaptive manufacturing operations, allowing machines to make real-time decisions and optimize processes with minimal human intervention. Furthermore, AI-driven systems enhance predictive capabilities, reduce downtime, improve product quality, and increase operational efficiency. The research also highlights the importance of human-machine collaboration, workforce skill development, and strategic planning to ensure successful AI integration. Beyond operational benefits, AI contributes to sustainable manufacturing by optimizing resource utilization, reducing energy consumption, and supporting environmentally responsible practices. The findings indicate that AI functions not only as a technological tool but as a strategic enabler that fosters innovation, agility, and resilience across manufacturing organizations. This study provides insights for industrial leaders, policymakers, and researchers on leveraging AI to achieve competitive advantage and drive sustainable growth in modern manufacturing environments.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes the Luxury Waterloo hypothesis, arguing that the global luxury market is undergoing structural segmentation following the post-pandemic boom. While the recovery in luxury demand has often been interpreted as a durable expansion of global consumption, this study suggests that the apparent boom may conceal a deeper transformation in the structure of luxury markets. Drawing on pricing developments and market observations among leading luxury houses such as Rolex, Cartier, Patek Philippe, and Van Cleef & Arpels, the analysis identifies persistent price escalation combined with increasing concentration of demand among ultra-high-net-worth consumers. The paper introduces the Luxury Pyramid Collapse Model, suggesting that rising entry thresholds and wealth concentration are gradually eroding the aspirational consumer base that historically supported luxury market expansion.

title: Dynamic Pricing with Consumer Urgency: Markup Paths and Inventory Disclosure

detail.title: Dynamic Pricing with Consumer Urgency: Markup Paths and Inventory Disclosure

keywords: deep reinforcement learning Dynamic Pricing with Consumer Urgency

detail.abstract: Empirical evidence from the hospitality and aviation industries consistently reveals a common pricing pattern: prices rise toward the end of the selling horizon. This pattern recurs across industries yet remains behaviorally under-explored by existing literature. Methodology/results: To investigate this phenomenon, we formalize consumer urgency, grounded in the psychology of "Fear of Missing Out," into a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process framework to model consumer behavioral dynamics. We derive a structural decomposition of the optimal pricing trajectory into three effects: the classical deadline effect and scarcity effect, and a newly identified urgency effect whereby intensifying consumer urgency enables the firm to charge higher prices. This urgency effect establishes a structural condition under which the optimal price path shifts from markdown to markup even between sales, thereby providing a theoretical foundation for the empirically observed late-stage price increases. Building on this, we propose inventory disclosure as an effective tool to intensify consumer urgency. We further show that the optimal disclosure policy is to reveal inventory if and only if the true inventory triggers a stronger urgency signal than consumers' urgency, and provably demonstrate the value of inventory disclosure. To solve the joint pricing and disclosure problem, we propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) based framework, and numerical results under both known distributions and real-world data-driven simulators validate our theoretical findings. Managerial implications: Our framework establishes consumer urgency as a behavioral driver of pricing dynamics and inventory disclosure as a strategic tool to actively manage it. The DRL-based framework further demonstrates that the urgency effect can be learned implicitly through iterative feedback without explicit input of the urgency dynamics, providing firms with a practical approach to leveraging consumer urgency for revenue optimization.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how immigration affects consumer prices. Using scanner data and instrumenting county-level immigration with historical ancestry patterns, we find that an inflow of 10,000 immigrants lowers four-year price growth by 0.58 percentage points. Leveraging variation in firm exposure through sales versus production locations, we show price declines stem entirely from the product demand channel: firms lower prices in response to immigrants in sales markets, not production locations. Evidence suggests that immigrants search more intensively, exhibit higher demand elasticity, pay lower prices for identical products, and shift expenditure toward lower-appeal products-consistent with a model of heterogeneous price sensitivity.

title: Why Artificial Intelligence Will Plateau - and Predictive Intelligence Will Replace It

detail.title: Why Artificial Intelligence Will Plateau - and Predictive Intelligence Will Replace It
detail.abstract: This paper advances a deliberately contrarian yet analytically grounded thesis: the dominant paradigm of Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly generative foundation models, is approaching diminishing returns across technological, economic, and epistemic dimensions. While recent advances have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in content generation, these systems remain structurally constrained by limitations in reliability, uncertainty calibration, and decision relevance. More fundamentally, current AI architectures lack mechanisms for grounded understanding-operating primarily on probabilistic pattern continuation rather than on causal, contextual, and semantically coherent representations of the world. As a result, the same systems that excel in generating plausible outputs often fail in supporting decision-making under uncertainty. Against this background, the paper introduces Predictive Intelligence (PI) as a distinct paradigm centered on probabilistic forecasting, causal reasoning, and decision optimization. It argues that future competitive advantage will depend not on generative capacity, but on the ability to anticipate outcomes, evaluate uncertainty, and derive validated Next Best Actions. The paper concludes that while generative AI will remain an important interface layer, the strategic core of intelligent systems will shift toward predictive, understanding-driven architectures.

title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Marketing and Changing Consumer Engagement and Consumer Behaviour

detail.title: Applications of Artificial Intelligence in Digital Marketing and Changing Consumer Engagement and Consumer Behaviour
detail.abstract: This descriptive and conceptual study explores the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in digital marketing and its profound impact on consumer engagement and behavior. As digital landscapes evolve, AI has emerged as a critical driver for personalization, predictive analytics, chatbots, and targeted advertising, fundamentally shifting how brands interact with audiences. The global AI in marketing market is experiencing exponential growth, valued at USD 19.50 billion in 2024 and projected to reach USD 179.99 billion by 2034, registering a Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 24.89%. This paper examines key AI applications-including machine learning, natural language processing, and big data analytics-that enable marketers to move from mass targeting to hyper-personalized, data-driven strategies. Furthermore, it analyzes how these technologies influence consumer decision-making processes, enhance customer satisfaction, and foster loyalty, while also addressing ethical challenges such as data privacy and algorithmic bias.

title: Social Media Impacts on Habit Formation and Factors Influencing Youth's Cognitive Thinking and Sleep Duration

detail.title: Social Media Impacts on Habit Formation and Factors Influencing Youth's Cognitive Thinking and Sleep Duration
detail.abstract: With social media in every aspect becoming a key part of our daily lives, this study aims to find potential reasons that affect youth's cognitive thinking and sleep habits caused by overuse of social media. This study also focuses on examining how social media is impacting their rest patterns, for e.g. their average time of sleep. Data for the study is evaluated through the Secondary method, which involves a literature review of previous publications where common questions are analysed related to social media impact and sleep patterns. The findings indicate that a significant relationship exists between the use of social media and its impact on youth and adolescent habit formation and rest patterns. There are factors such as:-FOMO, Dopamine-driven engagement contributes to prolonged screen timings. The study also indicates the possibility of positives which involve social interaction, communication and information sharing as key aspects while using social media. The research also emphasises the need for creating awareness and policies to control the usage of social media in the future.

title: Employee Satisfaction and IPO Performance: Evidence from the DACH Market

detail.title: Employee Satisfaction and IPO Performance: Evidence from the DACH Market
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether pre-IPO employee satisfaction ratings on Kununu—the dominant employer review platform in German-speaking countries—predict IPO performance in the DACH market (Germany, Austria, Switzerland). Following the methodology of Farhadi and Nanda (2021), I construct two principal component measures—QualityRating, capturing perceived employer quality, and OverSatisfaction, capturing idiosyncratic employee well-being—for 66 DACH IPOs between 2013 and 2024. Across eight return horizons and multiple regression specifications, I find no significant relationship between either measure and market-adjusted excess returns. These null results stand in contrast to U.S. Glassdoor evidence and suggest that employee-generated information on Kununu is not priced by investors in the DACH IPO market, possibly reflecting a less informationally eﬀicient use of online employer reviews in continental European capital markets.

detail.abstract:
This chapter uses criminal law enforcement as a point of departure to probe and assess concerns about the influence of trade secrecy in public governance. It begins by outlining how the ascent of privately developed technologies in law enforcement has generated three distinct areas of concern. First, trade secrecy often conflicts with the protection of individual rights. Second, trade secrecy also may undermine public knowledge or oversight. Third, private vendors may use trade secrecy and other doctrines to retain most of the knowledge and understanding about government decisions, effecting a form of epistemic capture.

To develop these concerns, the chapter uses the example of acoustic gunshot detection technology. Widely deployed in the United States, gunshot detection technology ripely illustrates the risks that government reliance on proprietary technology poses for individuals, for public oversight, and for government competency. Trade secrecy takes on a particularly worrisome form where it conceals information essential to an individual’s defense or freedom. But trade secrecy is not an inevitable knock-on effect of innovation. A comparison of two providers of gunshot detection technology—ShotSpotter and Flock Safety—shows that developers of similar technologies can have broadly different orientations toward secrecy and disclosure. The chapter concludes that existing approaches overemphasize the potential of litigation and individual rights of access to solve the problem of trade secrecy, while underestimating the challenges of addressing broader problems of information asymmetry and epistemic power.

title: Integrating Digital Product Passport into Garment Rental Operations: A Simulation-Based Analysis
affiliations: , University of Strathclyde, University of Strathclyde, University of Strathclyde, Advanced Clothing Solutions and University of Strathclyde

detail.title: Integrating Digital Product Passport into Garment Rental Operations: A Simulation-Based Analysis
detail.abstract: Garment rental systems rely on efficient laundry operations to sustain circular product lifecycles. However, routing decisions in rental cleaning processes are often reactive, leading to extended routing sequences, rework loops, and uneven equipment utilization. This study develops a discrete-event simulation framework that integrates Digital Product Passport (DPP) information as garment-level decision inputs influencing laundry routing logic. Updated usage and condition data in DPP are translated into condition-based routing instructions, allowing garments to bypass default routing logic depicted by probabilistic transitions. Using empirical RFID scan data, we compare scenarios with different proportions of garments carrying updated DPP routing information. Results show that DPP-enabled routing reduces routing length, improves the selection of cleaning methods, and could reshape workload distribution across equipment. However, rental performance gains are constrained by upstream and downstream processes(e.g, return handling and shipping), suggesting that DPP must be integrated across the entire rental cycle to fully realize implementation benefits.

title: When Technology Resists Governance: Material Properties and Herd Behavior in IT Governance Formation

detail.title: When Technology Resists Governance: Material Properties and Herd Behavior in IT Governance Formation
detail.abstract: The material properties of an IT artifact shape whether and how quickly organizations can develop governance for it. We study this in AI, whose opacity, autonomy, data dependency, and capacity for emergent behavior make it a critical case, and argue that when an artifact exhibits these properties, governance infrastructure cannot form through normal channels of accumulated practice and shared standards. Instead, regulatory signals trigger rapid imitative vocabulary adoption that outpaces substantive governance development. We test this framework using a text-analytic method that separates vocabulary convergence from substantive convergence in S&P 500 10-K filings (2018-2025). After the 2023 AI regulatory surge, vocabulary convergence substantially outpaced substantive change, and few firms describe formal AI governance structures despite near-universal risk vocabulary adoption. That the IT artifact's properties drive this response is the cleanest finding: the same firms, in the same period, showed no comparable response to a contemporaneous cybersecurity disclosure rule, and AI vocabulary converged far faster than cybersecurity vocabulary, an ordering corresponding directly to the degree to which each technology's properties resist stable risk characterization. Direct tests confirm herd behavior as the mechanism: firms with less AI knowledge herd more, low-AI sectors imitate high-AI vocabulary, and a policy reversal stalled the sector differential. We introduce a decomposition method that separately measures vocabulary and semantic convergence, applicable wherever IS researchers need to distinguish surfacelevel technology adoption from substantive organizational change. These findings extend IT governance theory into the pre-governance stage. Technologies vary in governability: the degree to which their material properties permit stable risk characterization. Before organizations can allocate decision rights or design governance structures, the technology must be governable.

title: Realized Network Value: A Micro-Level Model of Individual Platform Experience

detail.title: Realized Network Value: A Micro-Level Model of Individual Platform Experience
detail.abstract: Existing models of network value treat connections as interchangeable and predict that value scales monotonically with network size. These aggregate models cannot explain why the same platform benefits one user and overwhelms another. This paper shifts the unit of analysis from the network to the individual user, introducing the Realized Network Value Model, which decomposes individual platform value into social ties, platform functions, tie--function interactions, and emergent ties, subject to cognitive and experiential constraints. The model derives closed-form thresholds for optimal network size and feature count, recovering Metcalfe's Law under simplifying assumptions. Six formal propositions yield testable predictions; four are robust to both additive and multiplicative value aggregation, whereas the remaining two depend on additive structure, identifying the clearest empirical test between specifications. A dynamic agent-based simulation with a dormancy mechanism, in which inactive ties continue to generate cognitive cost, demonstrates that a single mechanism, a fixed attention budget with diminishing returns, produces the network size--tie strength tradeoff without being built into the model and provides a mechanistic explanation for persistent social signatures (allocation shape reflects value-function curvature, not loyalty to specific alters). Cross-platform parameterization generates testable predictions about active network sizes and dormancy patterns across five platforms. An equilibrium analysis reveals that tie--feature complementarity exceeds diminishing returns at calibrated parameters, predicting that multi-function platforms exhibit sustained co-escalation of ties and features until external constraints bind. A global sensitivity analysis identifies the negative exposure exponent as the most influential parameter, with constraint and platform design parameters significantly shaping realized value.

detail.abstract: This study examines the contemporaneous effects of cancer prevention on health and healthcare utilisation amongst cohabiting spouses. To address potential endogeneity, we conduct instrumental variable (IV) fixed effects regression approach, applied to panel data for cohabiting partners in Europe. We instrument individual preventive behaviour with spouses' engagement in preventive behaviours and perform bounding exercises to evaluate the plausibility of the exclusion restriction. In particular, we provide causal estimates for the effect of colon screening and mammography on healthcare use, including visits to general practitioners and specialists, hospitalisation and health outcomes, such as cancer diagnosis and self-assessed survival probability. Our findings indicate that engaging in preventive measures leads to an increase in visits to the general practitioner, an increase in the probability of specialist consultations, and hospitalisations among females. For males, however, colon screening increases the probability of visiting a specialist only. We conduct heterogeneity checks to show that these effects vary by levels of education.

title: Market Infrastructure as Surveillance, Surveillance as Market Infrastructure: The Ethics of Business Monitoring

detail.title: Market Infrastructure as Surveillance, Surveillance as Market Infrastructure: The Ethics of Business Monitoring
detail.abstract: Market infrastructure is surveillance. Credit bureaus, insurers, and platforms all track behavior, generate signals, and attach consequences. Yet the ethical literature has analyzed surveillance almost exclusively through the lens of domination, providing no framework for evaluating business monitoring that may serve the interests of the monitored. This paper addresses two questions. First, under what conditions is business surveillance ethically justified? We develop a seven-condition framework derived from four structural dimensions of any surveillance relationship. A key distinction is between penalty-based surveillance, which characterizes most business monitoring, and reward-based surveillance, which creates access to opportunities that would not otherwise exist. Second, where market infrastructure is absent, can ethical surveillance become that infrastructure? We argue that under four specified boundary conditions, it can: surveillance meeting the seven conditions can function as substitute market infrastructure, bridging trust gaps that institutional voids would otherwise leave unbridgeable. We develop the framework through three cases: China's Social Credit System as a state-imposed counterpoint, FICO credit scoring as the dominant business surveillance system in developed economies, and AVICS, a developmental behavioral scoring system built by AVODA Group in Uganda that generates creditworthiness signals for investors. FICO and AVICS provide the framework's sharpest comparative test: both are privatesector systems claiming to serve economic inclusion, yet they differ on precisely the structural conditions that matter most. The framework applies to any business surveillance system, from credit scoring to employee monitoring to platform ratings. The necessity argument applies where institutional voids are acute, including post-conflict economies, refugee integration, and informal sectors, where the alternative to ethical surveillance is not freedom from monitoring but exclusion from economic participation.

detail.abstract: In this study, we examine how microenterprises use Generative AI (GAI) and consider the ways it may affect their socioeconomic development. In doing so, we revisit the established IT for Development (IT4D) model and adapt it to reflect opportunity areas and cybersecurity considerations specific to GAI. We propose the Generative AI for Development (GAI4D) model as a way to analyze both how GAI adoption may strengthen microenterprise capabilities and where it may create vulnerabilities. GAI4D highlights how GAI can both strengthen microenterprise capabilities and introduce new vulnerabilities, producing both upward and downward spirals of growth. The model offers an early foundation for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand and support GAI use in resource constrained business settings.

title: AI Bubbles with Large Language Models
affiliations: University of Oxford - Oxford-Man Institute of Quantitative Finance, , The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) and

detail.title: AI Bubbles with Large Language Models
detail.abstract: AI agents participate in both rational and irrational bubbles. In a sequential bubble game, AI agents generate speculative trades even though there is a unique no-trade equilibrium. Increasing reasoning capacity reduces, but does not eliminate, such irrational bubbles. Chain-of-thought analysis shows that AI agents participate in irrational bubbles because they form incorrect beliefs through simplified expectations of the market, and they are sensitive to framing effects when forming their beliefs. When the environment admits both a no-trade equilibrium and a speculative bubble equilibrium, AI agents recognize this multiplicity and coordinate on the speculative equilibrium. Our results suggest that greater AI sophistication does not necessarily eliminate bubbles or improve market efficiency.

title: The Ragsdale Framework for Autonomization: The Effort Composition Model

detail.title: The Ragsdale Framework for Autonomization: The Effort Composition Model
detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Effort Composition Model, a predictive structural projection within the Ragsdale Framework for Autonomization (RFA). The model proposes that under conditions of structural readiness, operational energy within organizations will progressively redistribute from human actors to machine systems over a ten-year horizon. Rather than forecasting workforce displacement, the model describes where monitoring, coordination, supervision, and execution reside as organizations mature through the phases of Aspiration, Awareness, Alignment, Acceleration, and Autonomization. The redistribution follows a structured Replaceability Ladder, beginning with analytical and rule-based tasks and advancing toward orchestration and bounded enterprise governance. The Effort Composition Model introduces a measurable temporal gradient to the structural architecture of the RFA and establishes a falsifiable basis for empirical testing using data generated within Autonomous Operating Environments.

detail.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of hospitalisation and premature death globally, imposing substantial costs to individuals and health systems. Preventive strategy such as strengthening primary care is one way to reduce the burden of these diseases. This paper studies the effects of one such prevention program, the Primary Care Nursing Program (PCNPs) on the health and healthcare services among patients with congestive heart failure. PCNPs are out-of-hospital services that support patients and general practitioners (GPs) by increasing engagement and promoting integrated management. Exploiting enrolment timing, we apply a dynamic difference in differences to high-frequency individual-GP-linked administrative data from the Emilia Romagna region in Italy. We estimate that PCNP enrolment reduces hospitalisations and emergency admissions for heart attacks modestly, 0.5 and 1 percentage points, respectively, within two quarters, while increasing cardiologist visits and echocardiograms by 5 and 2.5 percentage points, respectively, immediately after enrolment. Results are driven by individuals whose GPs lacked nurse support and previously been subjected to no financial incentives for chronic disease management. Cost-benefit analysis results in cost saving between, euros 50 million and 67 million.

title: Recommendations for Implementing a Cost-Effective VA Loss Mitigation Program
affiliations: Housing Risk and Policy Advisors

detail.title: Recommendations for Implementing a Cost-Effective VA Loss Mitigation Program
detail.abstract:
The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) holds 25% of the risk of loss on VA-guaranteed mortgages. Therefore, VA has an economic interest in directing mortgage servicers to engage in home retention programs that will reduce the number of defaults on VA-guaranteed loans that transition to foreclosure and cause losses to the agency. For VA, the potential benefit of cost-effective home retention programs is significant: we estimate that the average disposition today would cost VA $73,750.

We propose three recommendations for the VA loss mitigation program:

1)    Adjust the VA loss mitigation program to incorporate the best practices from other government programs: delegate to servicers the authority to use VA’s loss mitigation waterfall; permit forbearance for up to 12 months, to be resolved using the new home retention waterfall; and require borrowers to complete a 3-month Trial Payment Plan to demonstrate affordability before any home retention solution becomes permanent and VA absorbs the cost.

2)    Structure the Partial Claim (PC) as a servicer advance secured by the first lien, rather than a subordinate lien, which will reduce the cost and risk of administering the PC program.

3)    Develop a waterfall with the following sequence of steps: lump-sum repayment; repayment plan, with a term of up to 24 month; for borrowers who can resume their original monthly payment, a 30-Year Modification if it can provide a payment reduction, otherwise a Standalone PC; for borrowers who need a payment reduction to make their mortgage affordable, an Up-to 40-Year Modification that targets a 25% reduction in monthly principal and interest (P&I) payment; if the target P&I payment cannot be reached, the home retention alternative that creates the lowest monthly payment should be offered.

Our recommendations would allow VA to structure home retention solutions that generate loan reperformance and avoid the high cost of dispositions, while providing delinquent VA borrowers with similar assistance measures available on other federally backed mortgages.

title: National Interest vs Global Responsibility: What Should Nations Choose?
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: National Interest vs Global Responsibility: What Should Nations Choose?
detail.abstract: This paper examines the tension between national interest and global responsibility in contemporary international relations. Realist theories argue that states mainly focus on survival and power. Liberal and constructivist thinkers place more importance on cooperation and shared norms in world politics. This study discusses both perspectives and uses real examples to show how countries deal with this dilemma. Issues such as climate diplomacy, humanitarian crises, and global health show that national interest and global responsibility often overlap. Governments may act to help others, but these actions can also serve their own long-term interests. In an interconnected world, foreign policy cannot focus only on domestic priorities. Countries often need to work with others to protect stability and security. The paper suggests that national interest and global responsibility do not always conflict. In many situations, they support each other. A stable international system can strengthen a country's own security and influence. For this reason, successful foreign policy often involves balancing national goals with cooperation in the wider global community.

title: Driving Change: The Impact of Low Emission Zones on Commuting Behaviors
affiliations: UCLouvain - UCLouvain Saint-Louis, University of Liège and

detail.title: Driving Change: The Impact of Low Emission Zones on Commuting Behaviors
detail.abstract: Low Emission Zones (LEZs) have emerged as a widely adopted policy instrument aimed at reducing urban air pollution by restricting access for the most polluting vehicles. While substantial research has examined their environmental effectiveness, comparatively little attention has been devoted to their impact on mobility behavior. Using a difference-indifferences strategy applied to Belgian commuter data, this paper estimates the causal effect of the Brussels LEZ on modal choice. Individuals living within the LEZ and commuting to workplaces outside the zone reduce car use by 5.8 pp and increase train use by 4.9 pp. These effects vary across income groups, public transport accessibility, and commuting distance.

title: Responsibility As Economic Primitive Five-Dimensional Thread Vectors for Measuring Causation
affiliations: and

detail.title: Responsibility As Economic Primitive Five-Dimensional Thread Vectors for Measuring Causation
detail.abstract: This paper proposes replacing property with responsibility as the foundational unit of economic and legal measurement. Property, we argue, is constitutively opaque. Its social function requires severing present holdings from the causal histories that produced them, and this severance makes it structurally impossible to distinguish legitimate exchange from extraction. That opacity is the condition of property's institutional operation, not a defect to be corrected. No reform, however structurally ambitious, can extract causal information from a system whose architecture suppresses it. In response, we develop a formal measurement system built on five base units, which we call thread vectors: Genesis (causal contribution), Sight (epistemic position), Sovereignty (capacity to intervene), Harvest (distribution of benefit and burden), and Restoration (capacity and obligation to repair). We demonstrate that these five dimensions are necessary together as much as they are sufficient to span the space of responsibility across the domains examined in this paper. We then develop the mathematics of their combination into weaves: calculable structures that enable forms of accountability no existing instrument achieves. These include the apportionment of systemic harms across distributed actors, the calibration of restitution to measured extraction, and the anticipatory detection of accumulating culpability.

detail.abstract: The study examines links between automated advisory services and irrational individual investors' behaviour based on dual-process theory. The study contributes to the literature on active vs. passive digital nudges in robo-advisors and the disposition effect. Selfreporting online experiment revealed that robo-advisors help investors to resolve cognitive dissonance, with passive robo-advisors being more efficient. We contribute by introducing and indicating the moderating role of financial literacy. Though moderating feminine gender role was not supported, the need for customized automated advisory services is highlighted. The results are important for individual welfare, as demographic shifts and evolving retirement systems transfer investment decisions to individuals.

title: Are Transition and Physical Climate Risks Priced? Evidence from Directional News-Based Measures

detail.title: Are Transition and Physical Climate Risks Priced? Evidence from Directional News-Based Measures
detail.abstract: I build directional climate risk indicators from over 100,000 news articles using a large language model. The measures distinguish transition from physical risk and, unlike existing indices, code whether news signals increasing or decreasing risk, as well as intensity and horizon. Transition-risk innovations are priced in the cross section, carrying a significantly negative risk premium, while higher transition risk predicts a deterioration in future investment opportunities, consistent with the ICAPM. This joint pricing–predictability pattern disappears when risk direction is ignored. Physical risk predicts aggregate returns but is not priced cross-sectionally, consistent with its localized nature.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author conducted the applied economic assessment of the anonymized case firm as an independent research engagement. The author has no financial interest in the case firm and received no compensation contingent on the outcomes of the analysis.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The applied economic assessment from which the case data is derived was conducted as an independent research engagement.

detail.abstract: The global managed security services market is growing at a compound annual rate exceeding 11 percent, with total cybersecurity spending projected to reach USD 240 billion by 2026. Despite these favorable demand conditions, a significant proportion of managed security service providers (MSSPs) operate at or near breakeven, exhibiting a persistent structural decoupling between market expansion and firm-level profitability. This paper develops and validates the Margin Trap Model, an economic governance framework that identifies three interacting structural mechanisms driving this phenomenon: (1) labor-proportional delivery architectures that prevent operating leverage, captured by the Delivery Leverage Ratio; (2) corporate overhead absorption that compresses enterprise-level EBIT even when service-level contribution margins are healthy, captured by the Overhead Absorption Rate; and (3) growth-governance misalignment where revenue targets systematically exceed the organic capacity of labor-bound delivery models, captured by the Growth-Governance Alignment index. The framework is validated through industry-level financial analysis of publicly listed cybersecurity firms and in-depth economic case analysis of an anonymized mid-market MSSP. The model demonstrates both explanatory power and prescriptive power, contributing the first formal economic model of MSSP profitability dynamics and proposing three monitorable governance variables for board-level oversight of cybersecurity services enterprises.

title:
Building a Resilience-Maximizing Societal System Through the Weekly Work 3+3 Scheme (WW33) and the Automated Value Transfer Tax (AVTT)

detail.title:
Building a Resilience-Maximizing Societal System Through the Weekly Work 3+3 Scheme (WW33) and the Automated Value Transfer Tax (AVTT) 
/ Transaction-Level Design, the Self-Harm Feedback Effect, and Real-Economy Resilience Under Price Dynamics

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper presents a theoretical and simulation-based analysis and does not involve human subjects research.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes an integrated institutional framework for a resilience-maximizing society that combines the Weekly Work 3+3 Scheme (WW33) with the Automated Value Transfer Tax (AVTT). The framework treats economic activity as a system of value transfers and designs policy levers at the transaction level, emphasizing automaticity, transparency, and robustness under shocks.

WW33 restructures the week into three days of primary work, three days of free activity, and one day of rest, while defining social protection at the individual level and decoupling entitlements from employment status. AVTT replaces conventional tax categories with an automatic, low-rate levy imposed at the moment of value transfer, and finances a universal, individual-based basic income.

Three simulation studies evaluate the framework under (i) economic attack and trade disruption, (ii) price volatility and purchasing-power protection using reserves and smoothing rules, and (iii) a gradual transition from an inflation-based economy with public debt under immediate versus phased implementation. The simulations indicate that economic aggression can generate a “self-harm feedback” effect that burdens the attacker before the target; that reserve-based operations can stabilize real purchasing power through adverse price shocks; and that full transition alongside debt redemption is feasible within approximately three decades under the assumptions explored. This proposal is put forward not as a policy program grounded in any particular ideology, but as technical and institutional infrastructure open to verification and refinement through insights from across disciplines.

title: Arbitrage-Free Construction of Volatility Surfaces in the Ultra-Short Tenor Regime: Applications to 0DTE Options and Stable Greeks Extraction

detail.title: Arbitrage-Free Construction of Volatility Surfaces in the Ultra-Short Tenor Regime: Applications to 0DTE Options and Stable Greeks Extraction
detail.abstract: We benchmark volatility surface construction methods for zero-days-to-expiry (0DTE) options using 414 trading days of tick-level NBBO SPY data spanning 148,380 unique evaluation minutes across multiple volatility regimes. Five methods (standard SSVI, cubic spline on implied volatility, cubic spline on total variance, constrained SSVI, and a flow-regularized variant) are evaluated against static arbitrage compliance and full-surface Greek stability. Two findings emerge. First, unconstrained interpolation fails catastrophically: cubic spline on implied volatility exhibits butterfly arbitrage violations in 99.98% of evaluated minutes, and cubic spline on total variance in 99.93%, with both achieving vanna volatility exceeding 164% at 25-delta. Second, at-the-money Greek metrics produce systematically misleading method rankings; cubic spline achieves the lowest ATM gamma volatility (11.1%) while exhibiting the worst wing stability. Constrained SSVI, enforcing butterfly no-arbitrage and calendar monotonicity, is the only method with explicit no-arbitrage guarantees that achieves zero arbitrage breaches and stable full-surface Greeks simultaneously.

detail.abstract: We derive useful tools to solve continuous-time infinite-horizon optimal control problems with unbounded payoffs, important in economic theory. We examine several general classes of such problems with unbounded payoffs, for which existing literature offers no sufficient condition allowing to conclude about optimal controls and value functions from the solutions of the HJB equations. We state sufficient conditions for the value function, optimal controls and ε-optimal controls. An essential part of this sufficient condition is a pair of terminal conditions checked along every admissible trajectory. We illustrate essentiality of the results with economic and ecological examples.

title: Operating-State Valuation Theory -Full Document Export
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Operating-State Valuation Theory -Full Document Export
detail.abstract: This paper develops a structural operating-state framework for corporate valuation grounded in economic profit identity and capital continuity principles. Rather than proposing a new valuation formula, the study reclassifies the source of intrinsic value by distinguishing economic spread generation from discounting mechanics. We formally demonstrate that firm value equals invested capital plus the present value of future economic surplus (EVA), and that traditional discounted cash flow (DCF) models are algebraically equivalent representations under consistent reinvestment assumptions. The analysis further establishes a structural invariance proposition showing that intrinsic value remains invariant under fixed versus time-varying WACC specifications when capital continuity and spread consistency hold. Beyond equivalence, the framework introduces incremental capital allocation conditions, demonstrating that expansion increases value if and only if incremental return exceeds the cost of capital. We extend the model to governance, credit analysis, and board-level capital discipline, showing how historical economic spread patterns reveal managerial capital allocation competence. The contribution is structural: valuation is reclassified as a discipline of economic spread stability and capital preservation rather than a discounting exercise. The framework integrates valuation identity, convergence properties, and institutional application into a unified theoretical structure.

title: Political Ecology of Farmer-Herder Conflict in West Africa: Climate Stress, Governance, and Rural Livelihoods
affiliations: National Open University of Nigeria, University of Nigeria, National Open University of Nigeria and Abia State Polytechnic

detail.title: Political Ecology of Farmer-Herder Conflict in West Africa: Climate Stress, Governance, and Rural Livelihoods
detail.abstract: The farmer-herder crisis has become the most prominent land resource conflict in the West African sub-region. Although research and government efforts at the national and regional levels have made significant policy advances toward peaceful coexistence between herders and farmers, the underlying dynamics driving the conflict are rarely addressed in policy measures. Achieving peaceful coexistence in areas with long-standing conflicts, deeply rooted ideologies, and sociopolitical affiliations requires understanding the specific context and perspectives of the conflicting parties. Using a mixed-methods approach, we combined qualitative and quantitative data in a convergent parallel design. We conducted an ordered logistic regression using a panel of geocoded conflict and survey data (Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project [ACLED] and Afrobarometer), along with satellite imagery (Landsat) processed with machine learning algorithms for land cover classification. We applied a standardized land cover classification to divide Nigeria into spatial units of 27 x 27 km, resulting in 1267 regions, each covering 729 km². We created cross-sectional data at the subnational administrative level. With this data, we examined how attitudes toward the political system, institutional structures, and economic variables at the individual level influence conflict occurrence. Our findings indicate that climate variables, political dynamics, and livelihood diversification significantly influence the likelihood of conflict in a given area. The complex relationships among weather factors, political conditions, and economic variables highlight the need to integrate climate adaptation, resource management, and conflict resolution policies to address farmer-herder conflicts.

title: Impact of Digital Twin Adoption on Food Supply Chain Performance: A System Dynamics Approach

detail.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology provides a promising solution to challenges within the food supply chain (FSC) due to its unique characteristics. While existing literature highlights the potential of DTs to enhance real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and operational efficiency, a quantitative assessment of the overall impact of DT implementation on FSC performance is missing. This study bridges this research gap by integrating experimental and analytical approaches. Empirical data were collected through questionnaires from food industry practitioners, combined with literature to develop a mental model for capturing the interrelationships among DT-relevant technologies, FSC operations, and supply chain performance. Later, by deploying systems thinking and system dynamics (SD) modelling approaches, the impact of DT adoption on FSC operational metrics is evaluated. The findings indicate that the DT positively impacts inventory levels, actual delay (lead time), and unfulfilled orders in the short term, while contributing to cost reduction and food waste in the long term. The SD models not only highlight the impact of integrative technology adoption on the operations of FSCs but also provide a comprehensive framework for modelling and assessing SC systems under the influence of technology. This study contributes by providing quantitative evidence of DT's impact on the FSC.

title: Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: Fudan University, Fudan University, Fudan University, Fudan University and Sun Yat-sen University (SYSU) - School of Business

detail.title: Long-Run Conditional Value-at-Risk Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) is a prominent risk measure in financial engineering, energy systems, and supply chain management. In these domains, Markov decision processes (MDPs) with a long-run CVaR criterion effectively mitigate cost variability over a specified horizon. However, implementing MDPs relies on known transition models, which are typically unavailable in practice. This necessitates a model-free approach to risk-sensitive dynamic optimization. To tackle this challenge, we propose a reinforcement learning algorithm that simultaneously conducts policy evaluation and improvement based on a CVaR-specific Bellman local optimality equation. This algorithm employs a nonparametric incremental learning approach for policy improvement, relying on a single sample trajectory to identify the optimal policy. Under appropriate technical conditions, we prove almost sure convergence of the algorithm and derive its convergence rate. Our analysis reveals that the optimal convergence rate, measured by the mean absolute error of policy estimators, is of order O(1/n). Our main algorithm and results are further extended to solving the mean-CVaR optimization problem. Numerical experiments corroborate these results.

detail.abstract: This paper aims to examine two recent legislative initiatives of the European Union (EU)-the 6th AML Directive and the new AML Regulation, focusing particularly on the provisions that reform targeted financial sanctions as part of the EU's anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) framework. The paper explores why the reform was considered necessary, highlights the key objectives and rules governing targeted financial sanctions in the context AML/CFT, and discusses the challenges, as well as the opportunities that arise. The article argues that the integration of TFS into AMLD6 and AMLR represents more than a technical adjustment. It transforms sanctions from primarily foreign-policy tools into core preventive obligations embedded in the compliance frameworks of public authorities and private actors. This reorientation, however, raises challenges of consistency, resource allocation, and rights protection that will ultimately determine the effectiveness of the EU's new sanctions architecture.

title: Information Quality and Consumer Search for Experience Goods: Evidence from Online Shopping for Cameras

detail.title: Information Quality and Consumer Search for Experience Goods: Evidence from Online Shopping for Cameras
detail.abstract: This paper develops and estimates a consumer search model for experience goods-products that are challenging to evaluate without direct use-available across multiple retailers. Beyond price uncertainty, consumers also face uncertainty about product suitability (match values) and form expectations about the quality of the match-value information available at different retailers, available for instance through consumer reviews. Consumers direct search across retailers based on their expectations about prices, retailer preferences, and expectations about match information quality. Consumers gain more precise match signals at retailers with higher quality match information, which makes finding a well-matched product more efficient. Analyzing clickstream data on camera searches, I document search behaviors that cannot be explained by models lacking expectations about information quality. Structural estimation indicates that larger retailers, such as Amazon and Walmart, provide higher-quality information, which I quantify enhances consumer welfare by 8.35%. Additionally, I show that retailers with superior information quality have an increased capacity to steer consumers and extract rents.

title: Periphery, State, and Territory: A Scoping Review of Entrepreneurship in Informal Settlements
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Periphery, State, and Territory: A Scoping Review of Entrepreneurship in Informal Settlements
detail.abstract: This scoping review maps a fragmented literature on entrepreneurship in favelas/informal settlements and theorizes a structural gap that existing lenses fail to capture. Following Arksey and O'Malley and PRISMA-ScR reporting, we screened major databases and inductively coded 46 studies. We synthesize six recurrent trends and advance the P-S-T (Periphery-State-Territory) framework as an integrative lens. Component P formalizes a pragmatic logic of effectuation and relational capital; S identifies an institutional contradiction in state/market inclusion, comprising programmatic misalignment and the hidden cost of segregation; T models territorial regulation by parallel power and hybrid illegality in rentier accumulation. The framework clarifies why interventions targeting individual agency routinely underperform when institutional and territorial constraints remain unaddressed. We outline a forward agenda prioritizing (i) longitudinal designs, (ii) crosscountry comparisons across the Global South, and (iii) systematic attention to technology, race, and gender. Overall, P-S-T offers a useful analytical scaffold to organize cumulative inquiry and to inform policies attuned to the governance realities of informal urban economies.

title: Elderly Care in the Post-Pandemic Era: Case Studies from Taipei, Toyama, and Hong Kong

detail.title: Elderly Care in the Post-Pandemic Era: Case Studies from Taipei, Toyama, and Hong Kong
detail.abstract:
The COVID-19 pandemic exposed significant vulnerabilities among aging urban populations, including limited healthcare access, social isolation, and economic insecurity. As the proportion of residents aged 65 and above continues to grow, cities face increasing pressure to incorporate age-inclusive strategies into urban planning. This paper examines how urban policies can address the needs of older adults while supporting broader economic and social development. Drawing on critiques of traditional “creative city” models that often overlook vulnerable populations, the study highlights alternative approaches emphasizing inclusivity, community networks, and accessible urban infrastructure.

Through case studies of Taipei, Toyama, and Hong Kong, the paper explores innovative initiatives such as senior volunteer networks, shared community dining, compact city transport systems, intergenerational care facilities, and lifelong learning programs. The findings show that effective responses combine physical infrastructure with social programs that strengthen community participation and intergenerational connections. These cases demonstrate how cities can leverage local resources and collaborative governance to enhance the health, independence, and social integration of older adults in post-pandemic urban environments.

detail.abstract:
Career Paths of the Permanent Education Press
This appendix accompanies the chapter, "The Permanent Education Press" in the book The Malfunction of U.S. Education Policy: Elite Misinformation, Disinformation, and Selfishness

Introduction and Guide 
The following charts illustrate two characteristics of the Permanent Education Press: the pervasiveness of funding from the Gates and allied foundations; and the flow in, out, and in-between allegedly independent and objective media platforms and research or advocacy organizations that make no promises about independence. For every Debra Viadero or Jay Mathews who has stayed with traditional news media for life, there is another journalist happy to work at organizations with agendas and no pretensions about preserving independence or objectivity. Which, in turn, makes one wonder about the objectivity of their previous work.

Another revealed characteristic: a generally Northeastern, elite academic background—Ivy League or equivalent. It may be more than coincidence, then, that some choose to rely on "go to" expert sources with similar academic backgrounds, to the exclusion of a large population of more experienced, and more specifically trained sources.

Members of the "Permanent Education Press" have large regional or national audiences and remain in the education "industry" for life. That loyalty to education topics should have advantages: they should get to know topics more deeply and, by following them over time, can compare against evolving backgrounds and changing contexts. But some also get stuck in ruts, … deeply. It is common for permanent education press members to rely exclusively on "go to" sources, thus skewing their coverage toward those sources' particular knowledge base, incentives, and biases. Moreover, their own community is tight and self-reinforcing; one journalist's "go to" source may be others' as well. Permanent Education Press groupthink is both profound and pervasive.

detail.abstract: We study how to recover and use demand elasticities in dynamic asset markets. In demand system asset pricing, any price movement is accompanied by changes in future expected prices, returns, and risk, so there is no single context-free elasticity. The instrumented elasticity, which captures the reduced-form response to a shock that moves prices together with the expected path of future returns, is shock-specific and depends on the attributes of the identifying variation. The structural elasticity, which holds all future objects fixed, is transportable across shock environments. We show that the inverse of the instrumented elasticity is the price multiplier under a weak exclusion restriction and characterize how multipliers vary with shock persistence, volatility, systematic exposure, and surprise content. We then develop a recovery theory that uses the impulse responses of flows and prices to extract the transportable structural demand coefficients from shock-specific reduced-form estimates. In weekly data, recovered structural elasticities of 4.3 to 6.2 far exceed the naive inverse-multiplier benchmark of 0.3 to 0.4.

title: Screening with Cash Deposits in Digital Credit Markets

detail.title: Screening with Cash Deposits in Digital Credit Markets
detail.abstract:
We study a loan contract that requires borrowers to make a temporary cash deposit prior to disbursement, which is fully refunded and does not alter repayment incentives. In a randomized controlled trial with a digital lender, applicants are offered otherwise identical loans with or without a deposit. The deposit requirement reduces loan take-up but substantially improves repayment and lender profitability. The results indicate that deposits screen borrowers on both observable and unobservable characteristics. Higher-risk borrowers are less likely to take up deposit loans, and among borrowers with the same observable risk profile, those who accept deposit loans repay at higher rates, with the largest differences among low-risk borrowers. These findings show that simple contract features can complement data-driven credit models by adding an additional screening margin.

title: Salience and (Non-)Buyer's Remorse: Optimal Nonlinear Pricing with Cognitively Constrained Consumers

detail.title: Salience and (Non-)Buyer's Remorse: Optimal Nonlinear Pricing with Cognitively Constrained Consumers
detail.abstract:
Nonlinear pricing theory predicts that firms can extract surplus by inducing heterogeneous consumers to self-sort across price contract offers that are ex-post optimal for them. We study subscription pricing when the frictionless sorting assumption fails. Using large-scale subscription experiments conducted by Lyft, we document systematic deviations from optimal self-selection: many high-demand consumers decline subscriptions that would have saved them money, while some subscribers fail to break even. We develop a structural model of intensive-margin demand in which consumers may exhibit salience failures, forecast errors about future demand, or impulsivity. We show that subscription uptake can be recast as one-sided noncompliance in a binary-instrument framework, allowing us to leverage LATE methods to identify counterfactual outcome distributions and a novel “uptake function” linking baseline outcomes to compliance behavior. Combining experimental price variation with this identification strategy, we recover utility primitives, demand heterogeneity, and behavioral parameters. Salience failures and forecast errors play quantitatively important roles. Counterfactual analyses show that optimal subscription pricing generates substantial gains relative to linear pricing, but these gains are highly sensitive to consumer deviations from ex-post optimal choice. Implementing nonlinear pricing therefore requires not only optimal contract design for consumer screening, but also coordinated efforts to mitigate behavioral frictions.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, virtual instruction reduced in-person support that may have helped high school students transition to college. The model predicts that trade shocks change CEO compensation through scale, volatility, and ability-magnification channels. detail.abstract: Genetics confer 2–3-fold higher obesity risk through inherited mechanisms affecting appetite and metabolism, with pathways particularly modifiable during the first 1,000 days of life. We leverage the end of UK sugar rationing in September 1953, a sharp discontinuity in early-life sugar exposure by conception date, to examine whether sugar restriction mitigates genetically determined obesity risk using UK Biobank data linking an obesity polygenic index with adiposity phenotypes. Without rationing, high genetic risk individuals had triple the obesity prevalence of low-risk counterparts. Restriction through age two narrowed this disparity by 40%, operating through visceral rather than general adiposity, and was concentrated among high-risk adults with above-median adiposity levels. Early nutritional environments can alter inherited obesity trajectories, pointing to targeted early-life interventions to reduce genetically determined health inequalities.

detail.title: Decoupling Dollar and Treasury Privilege
detail.abstract:
We document a strong decoupling between the convenience yield on the U.S. dollar and U.S. Treasuries. We measure the convenience of the U.S. dollar using covered interest parity (CIP) deviations between risk-free bank rates, such as secured overnight rates since the benchmark reform. In parallel, we measure the convenience of U.S. Treasury bonds through CIP deviations between government bond yields. We find a pronounced divergence between the two convenience measures in recent years: while the U.S. dollar exhibits strong convenience post-Global Financidecoupal Crisis, the U.S. Treasury convenience has not only declined substantially but has turned negative, most strongly so at medium- to long-term maturities. We argue that the relative supply of government bonds between the US and other developed markets is a key driver of the U.S. Treasury convenience compared to other government bonds. Finally, we present a simple framework with a constrained global financial intermediary to link dollar and Treasury convenience.

detail.title: Networked Information and Industrial Output: Evidence from Chile’s 1972 Truckers’ Strike
detail.abstract:
This paper examines Cybersyn — Chile's cybernetic coordination system under Salvador Allende — during the October 1972 national truckers' strike, which cut aggregate industrial output by roughly 9 percent. Using monthly data for twenty sectors and a calibrated CES–Leontief model, I construct sector-specific counterfactuals for the trucking shock. The four government-designated priority sectors outperform their structural predictions by an average of 17 index points; the priority–non-priority differential sits at the 90th percentile of a permutation null distribution (p = 0.100). Mitigation was selective: concentrated in sectors with state-enterprise ownership, simple supply chains, and military distribution support. Where coordination needs were greatest — food and beverages — priority designation provided no measurable protection. Cybersyn was more effective at protecting the sectors it was easiest to protect than those that most needed protecting: a partial vindication and a realistic assessment of its limits.

detail.title: Cash Transfers and Productive Inclusion: Evidence from Bolsa Familia
detail.abstract:
We study how cash transfers affect work and health. Exploiting an increase in the generosity of the world's largest cash-transfer program for the extremely poor, we show that the reform raised employment by 5 percent while sharply improving health: hospitalization fell 8 percent and mortality 14 percent, saving roughly 1,000 lives. These findings challenge the view that transfers reduce work. Instead, transfers can relax binding subsistence and health constraints, raise productivity, and expand labor supply. We formalize this mechanism in a model of productive inclusion and use it to evaluate welfare, yielding lessons for antipoverty policy design in low-income settings.

detail.title: The Hidden Cost of Stock Market Concentration: When Funds Hit Regulatory Limits
detail.abstract:
As stock market concentration has risen, regulatory limits on fund portfolio concentration have become increasingly binding, especially for large-cap growth funds. When funds approach these limits, they trim their largest holdings and reduce equity exposure. Funds perform worse when constrained. A constraint-based ownership measure predicts stock returns, particularly among the largest firms. These findings suggest that high market concentration can distort stock prices by limiting the ability of optimistic investors to scale their positions. Just like short-sale constraints can produce overpricing by limiting pessimistic investors' views, constraints on long positions can generate underpricing by suppressing optimists' views.

title: The Cold War and the U.S. Labor Market

detail.title: The Cold War and the U.S. Labor Market
detail.abstract:
We argue that the Cold War contributed to the inclusive growth of the post-war decades. On the labor-demand side, we isolate exogenous shifts in military procurement across states and firms. We show that military procurement increases manufacturing employment and reduces inequality. Overall, the 1950s-to-1990s decline in defense production explains roughly one-quarter of the decline in manufacturing employment and nearly one-tenth of the rise of top-ten income share. On the labor-supply side, the Cold-War-era draft removed millions of young men from the labor force, significantly reducing young male civilian unemployment. Military procurement also increased voter support for hawkish foreign policy.

title: Picking Winners: Industrial Policy and Monopoly
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - Vanderbilt Law School

detail.title: Picking Winners: Industrial Policy and Monopoly
detail.abstract:
There is a gap in law’s theory of how the government should respond to competition problems. Antitrust law covers competition problems stemming from ordinary market failure, while the law of regulated industries covers competition problems that arise from natural monopoly. But there is a third type of competition problem that has received scant attention: competition problems caused by the government’s own actions. Throughout U.S. history, and especially in the present era, the government has shaped markets by giving advantages to some firms over others—a version of industrial policy I call “picking winners.” Markets with government-selected winners look nothing like the perfectly competitive ideal. But nor do they necessarily call for regulated industry treatment. These are markets that would ultimately benefit from competition, even if there was only one leading firm available to win a contract, grant, or regulatory privilege when the government made its initial pick.

This Article details what goes wrong when the government picks winners, and develops a framework for eventually generating competition in markets where policy choices have–justifiably or not–undermined it in the first instance. The cost of picking winners involves dampened innovation, dependency between the government and its chosen firms, bailouts, and reduced resilience against shocks. I label this set of consequences “entrenchment.” The solution is anti-entrenchment industrial policy, an approach that accepts the inevitability of picking winners but seeks to dislodge or rotate those firms over time. Anti-entrenchment industrial policy has four key components: it incentivizes entry; demands that state-supported firms make modular investments so as to smooth rotation among firms; limits cross-subsidies so as to constrain the reach of picking winners; and ensures that recipient firms can survive without the government so as to make exit realistic. As a north star for industrial policy, the anti-entrenchment approach clarifies how the government can act decisively in pursuit of national economic priorities without sacrificing the competitive foundation of long-run dynamism.

title: The Effects of Fiscal News on Household Expectations and Spending: New Causal Evidence

detail.abstract:
We provide experimental evidence on how fiscal news shapes households’ expectations and spending behavior. Using a new survey of ~11,000 Korean individuals linked to automatically collected high-frequency spending data, we elicit respondents’ fiscal and macroeconomic beliefs and randomly provide them with one of five pieces of information about current public debt levels, fiscal deficits, and the government’s plans for deficit reduction. Exogenous increases in expected future public debt raise expected inflation and increase consumer spending. On the other hand, exogenous increases in expected fiscal balance raise expected output growth and have no significant effect on consumer spending.

title: Adaptive Enforcement with AI-Augmented Monitoring
affiliations: Department of Economics, USC Gould School of Law and Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute (RPI) - Lally School of Management

detail.title: Adaptive Enforcement with AI-Augmented Monitoring
detail.abstract:
We study a novel dynamic inspection game in which a regulator commits to a detection technology, and a regulated firm chooses whether to engage in harmful conduct and, if detected and sanctioned, whether to incur a redesign cost that generates a modified violation requiring renewed detection. In this adaptive environment, bounded sanctions give rise to three Markov perfect equilibria: full compliance, harm until recognition, and persistent redesign. We show that AI-augmented monitoring can shift the equilibrium from persistent redesign to harm until recognition, but only when regulatory investment crosses a regime-shifting threshold. Below this threshold, greater monitoring intensity may increase enforcement workload without reducing aggregate harm, as the regulator repeatedly detects adaptive violations while the firm continues to redesign. Thus, partial investments in AI monitoring can generate congestion rather than deterrence. When the firm can also adopt AI to reduce its redesign cost, the regulator’s deterrence threshold rises, reinforcing the strategic interaction between enforcement and evasion technologies. Moreover, congestion becomes particularly salient when AI-flagged violations require human review and regulatory review capacity is binding. In this case, the precision of AI triage—especially its false positive rate—matters as much as detection intensity. Enforcement effectiveness therefore depends not only on expanding detection, but also on allocating scarce human review resources efficiently.
