title: Knowledge Spillovers and Local Outcomes: An Existence Proof from the Establishment of the National Labs
affiliations: Case Western Reserve University - Department of Economics, Case Western Reserve University and Case Western Reserve University

detail.title: Knowledge Spillovers and Local Outcomes: An Existence Proof from the Establishment of the National Labs
detail.abstract:
We study the establishment of U.S. National Laboratories in the 1940s–1950s to estimate local spillovers from public research infrastructure. This setting allows us to causally identify such spillovers, for two reasons: 1) Lab sites were chosen largely for security and political reasons, rather than existing or potential innovative capability and 2) We identify runner-up locations using archival sources. We find several types of knowledge spillovers: Compared to control counties, Lab counties experience large and persistent increases in patenting by non-lab inventors; non-lab patents in the same county shift toward laboratories’ research fields and cite laboratory patents more frequently. Using newly digitized county data from 1936–1970, we find sustained increases in retail sales and household income. Linked 1940–1950 Census records show wage gains for pre-existing residents who remain in lab counties, with larger effects for college-educated workers. We find that cohorts exposed to laboratory establishment during school-age years attained more education, consistent with a human-capital channel. Spillovers arise despite extensive secrecy around early nuclear research, suggesting that co-location with public R&D can generate sizable local benefits even under restricted information flows.

title: Dynamic Adjustment to Trade Shocks
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego, World Bank Group, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Dynamic Adjustment to Trade Shocks
detail.abstract:
Global trade flows and supply chains adjust gradually. Empirical estimates of the trade elasticity for the short run are a fraction of those for the long run and suggest that trade is subject to substantive dynamic frictions. We develop a tractable framework that provides microfoundations for trade adjustment and rationalizes estimation of a time-varying trade elasticity. The model features forward-looking firms facing sticky sourcing choices and nests a version of the Eaton-Kortum model as a limiting long- run case. We calibrate the model and quantify the impacts of two events: the 2004 EU Eastern enlargement (an anticipated change) and the 2018 US-China trade war (an arguably unanticipated change). Our findings suggest that sourcing frictions and anticipation effects alter the time pattern of specialization, can result in short-term welfare losses but long-term gains, and can drive marked trade adjustments before anticipated shocks occur.

title: Planning under Diagnostic Uncertainty: Question-Driven Learning in the Age of AI
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics

detail.title: Planning under Diagnostic Uncertainty: Question-Driven Learning in the Age of AI
detail.abstract:
Many important economic decisions depend not only on acquiring information, but on determining which questions are worth asking before committing to an action. Individuals and organizations must organize inquiry: they select questions, interpret answers, and update beliefs in ways that determine whether decisive distinctions are identified or missed. Despite its importance, the organization of inquiry is largely absent from formal economic analysis.This paper studies decision-making under \emph{diagnostic uncertainty}, in which agents must learn not only about payoff-relevant states, but about which questions are informative. We develop a model in which agents choose questions sequentially prior to commitment, while facing uncertainty over a latent diagnostic structure that governs how questions generate answers. Before each inquiry step, agents may incur cognitive cost to refine beliefs about this diagnostic structure. The resulting problem is a finite-horizon dynamic program over inquiry, in which costly attention is allocated to belief transformations over diagnostic structure rather than directly to payoff-relevant states.Two canonical diagnostic geometries isolate distinct planning margins. In one, value depends on locating a decisive question; in the other, on maintaining a correct sequence of questions. Both environments admit closed-form solutions and yield a common representation in which optimal inquiry increases the probability of success relative to uninformed search.The framework identifies a distinct margin of economic behavior—planning under diagnostic uncertainty—that becomes increasingly important in environments where answers are abundant but the organization of inquiry remains scarce.

title: The Economics of Postdoctoral Researcher Positions

detail.title: The Economics of Postdoctoral Researcher Positions
detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the dramatic growth and evolving role of postdoctoral researchers in the U.S. scientific workforce from 1979 to 2023, highlighting a fourfold increase in postdoc numbers that outpaced growth in graduate students and faculty. We argue that this expansion reflects the fragmented nature of science funding, particularly the effects of the NIH budget doubling in the early 2000s, which increased both supply and demand for postdocs but ultimately worsened employment conditions. The chapter also explores the career outcomes of postdocs, noting limited economic returns outside academia and declining transitions to faculty roles. With recent declines in postdoc numbers, tightening immigration policies, and rising compensation, it seems likely that the U.S. may have reached “peak postdoc,” potentially leading to reduced future research output. The chapter concludes with a call for improved data and further research to better understand postdocs’ roles in scientific production and career development.

title: In the Fed’s Mind

detail.title: In the Fed’s Mind
detail.abstract:
Does the Federal Reserve react to all inflation equally? We systematically analyze FOMC meeting records from 1937 to 2025 to construct meeting-level measures of the Fed’s real-time attribution of inflation to demand and supply pressures. We document substantial variation in these narratives over time and show that, since Volcker, the Fed has responded more aggressively to perceived demand-driven inflation. Consistent with this asymmetry, supply pressures have more persistent effects on realized inflation, while demand pressures' impact dissipates quickly. Financial markets also reflect this distinction: demand imbalances primarily move risk-neutral yields, whereas supply imbalances raise term premia and equity risk premia.

title: Real Effects of Academic Research Revisited

detail.title: Real Effects of Academic Research Revisited
detail.abstract:
This Chapter surveys the findings of social science research on the contribution of universities to innovation and economic growth, both locally/regionally and globally. In the last several decades research has demonstrated universities’ causal effects through the mechanisms of knowledge creation, education and training of students, and technology transfer/entrepreneurship. The Chapter summarizes how the literature has studied each of these mechanisms, and how the findings have probed variation across disciplines and economic sectors. The depth and breadth of understanding have been advanced by new microdata and new methods of linking data across inventions, scientists and institutions, and by application of methods from network science. We emphasize that research has proven the importance of these effects on average, but to date has less to say about the determinants of success or failure in different contexts. These findings have implications for public policy to foster innovation both regionally and globally.

title: Trade, Labor Market Concentration, and Wages

detail.title: Trade, Labor Market Concentration, and Wages
detail.abstract:
I estimate the effect of trade on local labor market concentration and its implications for wages using employer-employee linked data and tariff shocks from Brazil’s trade liberalization. Trade increased concentration by 7%, an effect driven by firm exit and worker flows to surviving import-competing firms. Increased concentration reduced wage take-home shares—estimated at 50 cents on the dollar pre-shock—enough to offset small wage gains from reallocation, but did not meaningfully reduce wages on net. Most of the wage declines attributed to Brazil's trade liberalization resulted instead from reductions in the marginal revenue product of labor. Incorporating informality reveals substantial regional heterogeneity.

title: LLMs Under Risk: Interactive Bayesian Risk Modeling

detail.title: LLMs Under Risk: Interactive Bayesian Risk Modeling
detail.abstract: Financial risk modeling is entering a new paradigm in which artificial intelligence moves beyond information retrieval towards interactive reasoning. Modern large language models (LLMs) can synthesize heterogeneous information and propose hypotheses about changing market conditions, but their integration into risk models must remain transparent and probabilistically disciplined. This paper introduces Bayesian Interactive Reasoning (BIR), a framework that integrates AI reasoning into financial risk models in a principled way: the AI agent generates hypotheses based structured probabilistic views, while Bayesian updating remains the formal mechanism for integrating these views with market data. This design provides a disciplined approach for adopting LLMs in market risk modeling while preserving interpretability, calibration, & statistical rigor. The framework helps translate AI-generated reasoning into interpretable risk drivers, allowing risk managers to identify which market narratives are materially influencing the portfolio's risk. We develop the methodology and illustrate its application through a toy backtesting experiment 1 in equity portfolio risk modeling.

title: Digital Antitrust Collectivism

detail.title: Digital Antitrust Collectivism
detail.abstract:
Countervailing power from grassroots users has long been underexplored in digital antitrust debates. Recent large-scale users’ collective actions unfolded in cyberspace, such as X–Bluesky, TikTok–RedNote in the United States (U.S.), and Meituan–JD.com in China, have demonstrated a critical and novel possibility that collectively empowered users can generate countervailing power and effectively discipline those incumbent digital empires.  

This Article, different from traditional antitrust discourse, raises that possibility by proposing Digital Antitrust Collectivism to guide future institutional design. The main theoretical contribution of this Article is that it views widely discussed harms, such as weakened data protection, distorted content moderation, and algorithmic manipulation, as derivative harms of the vertical power gap between digital service providers and scattered users. It argues that the vertical power gap and horizontal competition deficits constitute more fundamental, structural market failures. They are two sides of the same coin, mutually reinforcing and jointly entrenching the platform dominance.  

This Article, to my knowledge, is the first to address digital antitrust problems through a vertical lens. Echoing John Kenneth Galbraith’s well-known recognition of vertically countervailing power in highly concentrated markets, this Article proposes a policy blueprint, the Collective User Empowerment Scheme (CUES), to ignite users’ countervailing power in digital industries. With five integral components—collective knowledge, collective bargaining, collective switching, collective data management, and collective offlining—CUES can bridge the vertical power gap between tech giants and powerless users by narrowing information asymmetry, flipping network effects, and reshaping the techno-political nexus.   

Economically, CUES will mitigate digital market failures, creating more opportunities for innovative startups and invigorating digital market competition that effectively disciplines incumbent businesses. Politically, CUES enables and enhances users’ “voice” and “exit” in the digital space governance that would otherwise be dominated by authoritarian rule. Users’ collective actions constitute a form of contentious politics, which reshapes the structural foundations of the digital common. As a result, CUES acts as the Sword of Damocles, effectively checking the power of digital empires. Ultimately, this research will offer U.S. and other democracies’ antitrust scholars and lawmakers a novel lens for understanding the digital market ecosystem and redesigning their governance approaches.

Enforcement reduced trips by non-compliant car users by 19 percentage points, while motorcycle trip reductions were limited except among younger riders. Affected motorcycle users mostly replaced vehicles with compliant models. Women, younger individuals, higher-educated respondents, and lower-income residents showed greater behavioural responses in terms of transport mode choice and compliance actions. Results highlight important heterogeneity in compliance and the need to consider equity in low-emission transport policies.

It analyzes key treaty issues-expropriation, performance requirements, umbrella clauses, and procedural hurdles such as "fork-in-the-road", "attribution", and disputing parties' qualification issues in international investment arbitration-using doctrinal and comparative treaty interpretation, while assessing whether Most-Favored-Nation treatment clauses (MFN) can address protection gaps. title: AI Secrets Registration
affiliations: School of Law, City University of Hong Kong

detail.title: AI Secrets Registration
detail.abstract:
The surprisingly rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its increasingly sweeping use across industries are testing the resilience of traditional intellectual property doctrines. Trade secret law is equally experiencing a doctrinal reshuffle as it becomes an important mechanism for protecting what this article terms “AI secrets.” While this protection incentivizes continuous innovation and sustains long-term investment, firms' unrestrained reliance on trade secrecy poses a pressing issue: it legally constructs an opacity that severely exacerbates AI transparency concerns and constrains meaningful stakeholder scrutiny.

Current scholarship and regulatory responses primarily rely on mandated-disclosure approaches to reconcile this tension. However, this article argues that these approaches are inherently limited because the conflict between AI secrets and transparency is rooted in the structural features of trade secret law itself—notably, the inherent indeterminacy of its scope. Because the boundaries of protectable trade secrets are not fixed ex ante but are instead determined only through ex post judicial decisions, firms can unilaterally overclaim secrecy, effectively shielding even non-secret information from public scrutiny unless and until a court intervenes.

To address these structural failures and supplement current regulatory approaches, this article proposes a structural redesign of trade secret law when applied to AI secrets: a formal AI secrets registration system. Drawing on comparative insights from existing registration, recordation, and third-party review mechanisms in representative jurisdictions, specifically the U.S. copyright registration system, China’s local data registration systems, and the European Union’s AI and data governance frameworks, this article develops a conceptually grounded and pragmatically adaptable proposal. Ultimately, this foundational framework aims to facilitate future global implementation, offering a viable structural solution to resolve the transnational tension between AI secrecy and transparency demands while achieving ancillary benefits.

title: Licensing, Liability, and the Speed of AI Displacement: Legal Determinants of Labour Market Impact
affiliations: Sungkyunkwan University

detail.title: Licensing, Liability, and the Speed of AI Displacement: Legal Determinants of Labour Market Impact
detail.abstract: ﻿The debate over AI governance is organised around whether existing law suffices or new AI-specific legislation is needed. Yet neither side has systematically examined how existing legal structures already shape the speed of AI-driven labour market change across occupations. This paper develops a five-variable analytical framework – Technical Maturity, Error Cost and Liability Structure, User Entry Barrier, Regulatory Monopoly, and Adoption Decision-Maker Incentive – to explain why occupations with similar levels of AI capability may nonetheless experience very different timelines of displacement. Drawing on seven occupational sectors and Korean legal and accounting market data rarely examined in English-language scholarship, the paper generates five testable hypotheses and reframes current AI governance debates by focusing attention on the regulatory baseline already in operation.

title: Do Taxes or Age Explain Retail Dividend Clienteles?
affiliations: University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Kenan-Flagler Business School

detail.title: Do Taxes or Age Explain Retail Dividend Clienteles?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: William Yoder has no competing interests to disclose.

detail.abstract: I examine the relative importance of age and tax effects in explaining dividend clienteles among retail investors. Prior work draws inferences from limited datasets that confound age and tax status, typically focusing on older low-tax and younger high-tax investors. To address these shortcomings, I use comprehensive administrative data covering all taxable U.S. stock trades by 105 million individuals from 1999 to 2022, allowing a joint test of age and tax effects in the modern retail trading environment. I find that age-driven clienteles are nearly twice as strong as tax-driven clienteles. I conclude that tax considerations are second order and update our understanding of dividend clienteles in modern markets.

title: Cheering for a Constrained Maximization Problem
affiliations: Southern Methodist University (SMU)

detail.title: Cheering for a Constrained Maximization Problem
detail.abstract: Commentary on Major League Baseball has taken a turn towards viewing it adversarially between labor and capital, with labor as the protagonist. This paper develops a rational choice description of the labor market institutions of baseball as a combination of the league evolving as means of taming externalities that arise from incentives for overinvestment and a labor union to check the cartel. Unions in sport are viewed favorably as endogenously emerging as solutions to specific problems. However, inducing owners to spend more on labor will result in changes to future rules in labor agreements. Conventional fandom seeking teams to behave efficiently, or maximizing under a constraint, is argued to be a more coherent means of analyzing (and cheering) team behavior, and it does not amount to cheering for owners to profit.

title: Cutting Back to Move Forward: How Reduced Training Curbs Procrastination
affiliations: City University London - Department of Economics, Boston University, National Research University Higher School of Economics (Moscow) - International College of Economics and Finance and City, University of London

detail.title: Cutting Back to Move Forward: How Reduced Training Curbs Procrastination
detail.abstract: We study a dynamic moral hazard model without monetary transfers, in which a principal can gradually and costlessly transfer knowledge to raise an agent's productivity. Although transferring knowledge is efficient, the principal may deliberately limit it to deter the agent's procrastination, and this inefficiency persists even with infinite patience. Small differences in effort cost or learning rate can generate starkly different outcomes: one agent is made minimally productive, while the other receives maximal training. Commitment has no value for the principal, who can achieve her commitment-optimal payoff via a three-phase training with a mid-career dip, consistent with empirical evidence.

title: Representational Alignment for Multimodal Distracted Driving Detection: Parameter-efficient Adaptation of a Unified Embedding Space
affiliations: University of Memphis, University of Memphis, University of Memphis, University of Memphis and North Dakota State University

detail.title: Representational Alignment for Multimodal Distracted Driving Detection: Parameter-efficient Adaptation of a Unified Embedding Space
detail.abstract: Distracted driving remains a leading contributor to road traffic fatalities, yet most detection frameworks rely on limited unimodal or bimodal sensing that cannot reliably distinguish hazardous distraction from contextually appropriate behavior. Audio signals, which encode in-cabin events such as phone conversations and passenger interactions, remain largely excluded despite their potential to capture behavioral cues unavailable in video or vehicle telemetry. This study reframes multimodal distracted driving detection as a representational alignment problem and leverages ImageBind, a pretrained foundation model that projects vision, audio, and inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals into a shared embedding space, to evaluate whether parameter-efficient adaptation (LoRA) improves cross-modal compatibility for fine-grained distraction classification. Experiments on 733 naturalistic driving segments show that frozen embeddings achieve strong vision-only performance (Macro-F1 = 0.792) but yield no multimodal improvement, indicating that pretrained cross-modal alignment does not automatically translate to task-specific discrimination. Supervised contrastive adaptation improves performance to 0.821 Macro-F1 under weighted vision-audio fusion, a 2.9 percentage point gain concentrated in multimodal rather than unimodal configurations. Modality-aware weighted fusion consistently outperforms equal-weight strategies, highlighting the importance of accounting for modality imbalance. Class-level analysis further shows that multimodal gains are behavior-dependent, with the largest improvements observed in visually ambiguous categories such as eating/drinking and grooming, where acoustic context aids disambiguation. These findings demonstrate that effective multimodal distracted driving detection depends on representation quality rather than architectural complexity, and provide practical guidance for designing robust, context-aware driver monitoring systems with improved reliability in real-world driving environments.

title: Law and AI in Hiring: Lessons from the EU on Reconceptualizing Risks and Rights
affiliations: Leiden University, University of Luxembourg, IE University - IE Law School, New York University (NYU) - Jean Monnet Center and Leiden University

detail.title: Law and AI in Hiring: Lessons from the EU on Reconceptualizing Risks and Rights

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This article is part of an ILR Review Special Issue on AI and the Future of Work: Institutions. The article is also part of the ILR Review’s ongoing Policy Paper Series.
declarations.funderStatement: Rigotti and Fosch-Villaronga are thankful to the Horizon Europe BIAS Project that funded this project and received funding from the European Union with Grant Agreement Number 101070468. Aloisi’s contribution is made within the framework of the project PID2023-149184OB-C43 granted by MCIU / AEI / 10.13039/501100011033 and the FSE+ and forms part of the research activities of the Pérez-Llorca/IE Chair at the IE University Law School.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to streamline hiring procedures, but it raises concerns about transparency and discrimination. The European Union (EU)’s Artificial Intelligence Act (AIA) is the first broad attempt to regulate AI, using a tiered approach based on levels of risk. This article asks whether and to what extent such an approach can adequately protect job applicants’ fundamental rights. Focusing on the EU as a global reference point, it shows how connecting risk management with rights protection can make regulation more effective. The authors argue that involving affected groups through stakeholder-driven standardization, fundamental rights impact assessments, and co-determination can turn compliance from a box-ticking exercise into meaningful accountability. Placing the AIA within the broader contexts of data protection, equality, and product safety law, the article offers practical lessons for jurisdictions worldwide seeking to align technological innovation with fundamental rights protection.

title: The Good Life Euston Index Methodology
affiliations: University College London - Institute for Global Prosperity, University College London - Institute for Global Prosperity, University College London - Institute for Global Prosperity and University College London - Institute for Global Prosperity

detail.title: The Good Life Euston Index Methodology
detail.abstract: The Good Life Euston Index (GLEI) measures multidimensional prosperity across 12 Lower Super Output Areas in the Euston area of Camden, London. Developed by the Institute for Global Prosperity (IGP) at UCL, the GLEI is the third iteration of IGP's Prosperity Index framework, following the Citizen Prosperity Index (CPI) in East London and the Maisha Bora Index (MBI) in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The Index moves beyond conventional economic indicators to incorporate eight domains of prosperity derived from participatory research with local residents. Twenty-two trained citizen social scientists conducted qualitative research identifying the determinants of a good life, which were then translated into a household survey administered to 3,172 respondents across seven local areas surrounding Euston Station between September 2024 and March 2025. To address high non-response rates on income questions, a two-stage imputation procedure combines k-nearest neighbour methods with an XGBoost machine learning pipeline. Post-stratification weighting aligned to Census 2021 demographics ensures representative results. The Index follows a hierarchical aggregation structure in which survey measures are standardised via z-scores, combined into indicators and subdomains, and normalised to a 0-10 scale. The GLEI provides a benchmark for assessing regeneration outcomes against locally defined priorities and contributes to the growing literature on participatory, locally grounded prosperity measurement.

title: Wage Inequalities to Comprehend Gender Differences: An Analysis in the lenses of Surplus Value
affiliations: Jain (Deemed to be University)

detail.title: Wage Inequalities to Comprehend Gender Differences: An Analysis in the lenses of Surplus Value
detail.abstract: Despite millions of women entering the workforce, Hegewisch and DuMonthier (2016) found that women are paid 79 cents for every $1 paid to males. However, there is no substantial evidence of economic discrimination against women because this data is uncorrected for factors other than gender that might influence salaries, such as years of schooling, the choice of occupation, job experience, energy, contentment, ambition, geography etc... The general scientific belief remains that the gender wage gap is caused by free voluntary decisions of both genders and not by biased discrimination. This research is conducted upon the basis of identifying all plausible reasons behind the gender pay gap and to spotlight the pivotal reasons behind it.

title: GI Tags and Rural Development: Do Geographical Indications Actually Benefit Artisans and Farmers?
affiliations: Gujarat National Law University, Silvassa

detail.title: GI Tags and Rural Development: Do Geographical Indications Actually Benefit Artisans and Farmers?
detail.abstract: Geographical Indication (GI) protections under India's Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, adopted to implement the TRIPS Agreement, are intended to align intellectual property rights with socioeconomic goals such as rural development and the protection of traditional knowledge, yet the degree to which GI registrations actually benefit artisan and farmer communities is disputed. This paper examines this issue and evaluates whether the GI regime fulfils its promise of rural economic uplift and the protection of traditional knowledge. Employing doctrinal legal analysis and illustrative case studies Darjeeling Tea and Pochampally Ikat the research reviews relevant statutes, TRIPS obligations, and case law to assess the practical impact of GI registration on rural producers. The analysis finds that while GI designation can reinforce product identity and command price premiums, actual benefits for local communities are often limited by enforcement gaps, low producer awareness, inadequate marketing infrastructure, and weak institutional support. Case studies indicate that active producer participation through authorised-user schemes and the implementation of rigorous quality-control plans are critical to realising the promised gains. The paper argues that GI status alone is insufficient to guarantee rural development; effective community governance, formal qualitycontrol mechanisms, and integration with development support programmes are essential to translate intellectual property protections into tangible gains. By adopting a normative, evaluative approach, the study contributes to intellectual property law scholarship by linking GI policy to socioeconomic objectives and proposing recommendations to enhance the GI framework so that it better serves traditional producers and rural economies.

title: The Paradox of Gold Reserves: How Foreign Central Banks' Gold Holdings Create Indirect Exposure to U.S. Treasuries
affiliations: ESPM Sao Paulo-Brazil

detail.title: The Paradox of Gold Reserves: How Foreign Central Banks' Gold Holdings Create Indirect Exposure to U.S. Treasuries
detail.abstract: Foreign central banks are buying gold at the fastest pace in decades, widely interpreted as a strategic retreat from the U.S. dollar. This paper challenges that narrative. I argue that gold accumulation, far from constituting an escape from dollar hegemony, creates a web of indirect structural exposure to U.S. Treasuries through seven channels: the anchor effect of dominant U.S. gold reserves; the COMEX's control of global price discovery; the dollar-denomination of virtually all gold transactions; custodial arrangements at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; historical path dependencies rooted in Bretton Woods; the persistent gold–Treasury yield nexus; and the emerging role of dollar-backed stablecoins as substitute Treasury buyers. Crucially, I distinguish between two forms of exposure. Operational exposure refers to gold's structural dependence on U.S.-controlled infrastructure for pricing, trading, custody, and settlement. Return-correlation exposure refers to the sensitivity of gold's price to U.S. monetary policy, real yields, and fiscal conditions. While the latter has historically been inverse (gold rises when Treasuries fall), the post-2022 breakdown of this relationship, driven by concurrent fiscal stress, demonstrates that both assets increasingly respond to the same systemic risk factors. Drawing on data from the World Gold Council, the Federal Reserve (including IFDP No. 1420), the IMF's COFER database, the CME Group, the BIS, and recent academic literature, I find that gold reserve accumulation is best understood not as de-dollarization, but as an imperfect hedge that remains embedded within the American financial ecosystem, one that diversifies away from specific Treasury risks (credit, sanctions, freezing) while remaining tethered to the systemic infrastructure of dollar dominance. The paper concludes by examining whether Bitcoin, a decentralized, jurisdiction-neutral asset with permissionless settlement, resolves the structural dependencies that gold cannot, and argues that the combination of repatriated gold and self-custodied Bitcoin may represent the most robust sovereign reserve strategy currently available for nations seeking genuine neutrality from dollar-system infrastructure.

title: Gatekeepers and Self-Preferencing: Incentives and Welfare Trade-offs in Two-sided Markets
affiliations: Bocconi University - Department of Economics and Bocconi University

detail.title: Gatekeepers and Self-Preferencing: Incentives and Welfare Trade-offs in Two-sided Markets

declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge the financial support of the EODS research grant and the ERC Consolidator Grant “CoDiM” (GA No: 101002867).

detail.abstract: We study a two-sided platform where a dominant gatekeeper supplies both a primary product and a complementary ancillary service. By degrading outcomes for users of rival ancillary services, the gatekeeper engages in cross-market self-preferencing. Our theoretical model identifies when such behavior raises or lowers welfare, depending on buyers' and sellers' preferences and the platform's pricing instruments. Analyzing a recent antitrust case against Google, we show that remedies targeting only one side can misalign incentives between different user groups, reducing welfare. Counterfactual simulations highlight when alternative behavioral or structural interventions realign incentives and improve market efficiency.

title: Twenty Thousand Leases under the Sea? The Ongoing Failure of the International Seabed Authority to Prepare for the Exploitation Phase of Deep Seabed Mining

detail.title: Twenty Thousand Leases under the Sea? The Ongoing Failure of the International Seabed Authority to Prepare for the Exploitation Phase of Deep Seabed Mining

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted to appear in the Nevada Law Journal, 27 Nevada L.J. ___ (2026).

detail.abstract: For a century and a half, oceanographers have known that vast mineral wealth lies on the ocean floor in the form of polymetallic nodules.2 A century after the discovery of the nodules, as the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) was being negotiated, human access remained nearly impossible. Economic and technological obstacles to mining under three miles of ocean meant the nodules had remained undisturbed in their cold, dark home, under crushing pressure that rendered exploitation of this resource infeasible.3 Nonetheless, UNCLOS took into consideration the likelihood that a combination of technological progress and increasing prices for metals would eventually bring the seabed polymetallic nodules within the reach of the global economy. The result was UNCLOS Part XI, the framework of a code of law to govern deep seabed mining.

title: Matching in Vertical Markets: Evidence from the Digital Advertising Industry
affiliations: Università Bocconi, Bocconi University - Department of Economics, University of London, Royal Holloway College - Department of Economics, Universitat Pompeu Fabra (UPF) and Bocconi University

detail.title: Matching in Vertical Markets: Evidence from the Digital Advertising Industry

declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the ERC Consolidator Grant- CoDiM-#101002867.

detail.abstract: The digital advertising industry relies on specialized intermediaries to facilitate advertisers' access to online ad space. This paper studies vertical complementarities in this market by estimating a structural model of advertiser-agency matching using novel data and methods for many-to-many matching in large markets. We quantify the value created by matches and introduce a machine-learning approach to infer agents' consideration sets. The results show that advertisers benefit from being affiliated with the same agency network as their competitors, even though they do not necessarily prefer to share the same agencies. We also document the role of industry specialization, exclusive contracting, and relationship persistence. Finally, we illustrate the policy relevance of our framework by evaluating the potential effects of the Omnicom-IPG merger, showing how network-level consolidation can generate heterogeneous advertiser gains.

title: Rethinking Trend Following: Optimal Regime-Dependent Allocation
affiliations: University of Agder - School of Business and Law

detail.title: Rethinking Trend Following: Optimal Regime-Dependent Allocation
detail.abstract: We propose a simple and transparent theoretical framework for optimal regime-dependent allocation in trend-following strategies. While the existing literature on time-series momentum and related approaches focuses primarily on signal construction, portfolio exposures are typically imposed exogenously. In contrast, we treat detected market regimes as conditioning information and derive regime-specific asset exposures directly from a Sharpe-ratio maximization problem. The resulting allocation rule is fully tractable, applies to an arbitrary number of market regimes, and nests standard trend-following strategies as special, and generally suboptimal, cases. Using U.S. equity portfolios, international equity indices, and a broad set of diversified portfolio datasets, we show that optimal regime-dependent allocation delivers economically meaningful and robust improvements in out-of-sample risk-adjusted performance relative to the time-series momentum strategy of Moskowitz, Ooi, and Pedersen (2012) and the dynamic speed momentum strategy of Goulding, Harvey, and Mazzoleni (2023). These gains persist across assets and portfolio implementations, highlighting the central role of optimal positioning in trend following.

title: Hedging as a Liquidity Risk Management Strategy for Optimal Liquidation
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Hedging as a Liquidity Risk Management Strategy for Optimal Liquidation
detail.abstract:
In this research paper, we develop a comprehensive liquidation methodology for financial assets including semi-liquid structured credit and illiquid fixed assets. We start with a revision of liquidity metrics, developing a Liquidity Value at Risk metric for determining optimal liquidation, then develop a Waterfall approach for an exponential unwind of assets, that we present in a Liquidity Report for a hypothetical Global Rates fund as a final deliverable summary of the techniques developed. We also develop a methodology for a Constrained proportional unwind of assets with heterogeneous liquidity attributes; we encounter a bottleneck paradox in liquidation being dominated by the least liquid asset, even when it is a minority holding. We solve this problem with a Hedged Hibernation approach, whereby we acquire offsetting hedges collateralised and self-financed by the liquidation assets, in order to mitigate the risk of market uncertainty during the liquidation interval. We add this approach to the Liquidity Report to showcase a reduction in overall risk by 80% compared to an outright liquidation.

We review some of the limitations of a Hedged Hibernation Liquidation, establishing main constraints regarding leverage, interim funding, and complete markets regarding alternative hedging instruments. We look at the boundary conditions for a good hedge, in terms of correlation, time to liquidation, underlying volatility of the outright liquidation asset, and the residual basis risk that constitutes the Hedged Liquidity Value at Risk, and create a general framework for a Hedged LVaR risk function applying to both liquid and illiquid portfolios with constraints. We evidence how this general Hedged Hibernation Liquidation framework can be used for Private Markets, most specifically Semi-Liquid Credit, Private Credit, Infrastructure, and Real Estate.

title: A Race-dependent Internship Programme Operating at the Bar in England and Wales: An Analysis of the Legal Basis under the Equality Act 2010
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: A Race-dependent Internship Programme Operating at the Bar in England and Wales: An Analysis of the Legal Basis under the Equality Act 2010
detail.abstract:
This paper examines the legal basis, under the Equality Act 2010, for the 10,000 Black Interns programme. The paper includes an analysis of the statutory framework, and identifies the provisions that may apply to the programme. 

The paper proceeds by first outlining the publicly available information regarding the structure and operation of the programme. It then considers the relevant statutory framework and the circumstances in which differential treatment on the basis of a protected characteristic may be lawful. Finally, it draws some conclusions, and makes suggestions as to how greater clarity may be provided as to the lawful basis of the scheme.

detail.abstract: Microsoft SharePoint has become the backbone of enterprise collaboration, with over 200 million active users worldwide (Microsoft, 2023). Yet its very openness, the feature that makes it indispensable, also makes it one of the most persistent sources of unintentional personal information (PI) exposure. This article provides a practitioner-level framework for SharePoint privacy governance, drawing on authoritative guidance from NIST, GDPR Articles, CCPA, HIPAA, and Microsoft's own Purview compliance toolset. It argues that effective PI management in SharePoint requires not only technical configurations but a sustained governance culture that places data ownership, classification, and lifecycle management at the heart of everyday business operations.

title: Rethinking AI-generated Invention and Patent Protection
affiliations: Fordham University, School of Law

detail.title: Rethinking AI-generated Invention and Patent Protection

contentType.other: A Book chapter that was confirmed to publication at Cambridge Handbook of Generative AI and IP

detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the profound challenges posed by the invalidation of patent protection to inventions generated by artificial intelligence (AI) systems, with particular emphasis on the implications for innovation, market dynamics, and the doctrinal coherence of patent law. While a minority of jurisdictions acknowledged permissive recognition of AI as inventor, the dominant global approach continues to insist on human-only inventorship. Courts and patent offices have largely avoided substantive engagement with the economic and technological realities of autonomous invention, thereby entrenching a legal framework misaligned with contemporary innovation practices and causing economic harm. 

Drawing on comparative case studies-especially the global litigation surrounding the "DABUS" patent applications-the chapter explores how rigid adherence to human inventorship undermines the goals of the patent system: incentivizing innovation, ensuring fair competition, and promoting disclosure for the benefit of the public. Denial of patent protection for AIgenerated inventions exacerbates free-rider problems, creates market distortions, chills private R&D investment, and risks reshaping innovation economies, particularly in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, and advanced technology in general. The analysis situates these developments within broader law-and-economics discourse, emphasizing that uncertainty in patent eligibility impedes technological progress and diminishes national competitiveness. Ultimately, the chapter argues that voiding AI-generated patents constitutes a fundamental error in legal reasoning, policy design, and economic perspective. It calls for a rethinking of patent law to align with the realities of generative and autonomous technologies, drawing lessons from copyright's adaptive frameworks. U.S. courts have already embraced the proposed approach through the development of the 'Lion's Share' test, and in a similar vein, the Swiss Federal Administrative Court has recognized DABUS's inventorship by designating Dr. Stephen Thaler as the legal inventor in light of his substantial contributions, including programming DABUS and providing the underlying data. Policy solutions are proposed to reconcile inventorship doctrine with technological transformation, ensuring that intellectual property law in general and in particular patent law continue to fulfill its foundational mission of advancing science, innovation, and economic welfare.

title: Study on Asymmetry Stress Factor in Girth Welds of Sloped Pipelines Driven by Machine Learning
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, China University of Petroleum (East China), China University of Petroleum (East China), affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Study on Asymmetry Stress Factor in Girth Welds of Sloped Pipelines Driven by Machine Learning
detail.abstract: Sloped pipelines are a primary energy transportation method, yet pipeline failures caused by stress asymmetry have emerged as a critical challenge. The unique slope factors and welding process factors of sloped pipelines contribute to the complexity of asymmetry stress factors. Addressing this complexity requires a framework capable of capturing the relationships among these three factors. In this study, a database encompassing slope factors, welding process factors, and asymmetry stress factors is first established via numerical simulation and validated through experiments. Subsequently, a Long Short-Term Memory-Residual Network-Diffusion Model is constructed. Features of welding process factors and slope factors are extracted by bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory and Residual Network, respectively, and the diffusion model is employed to predict asymmetry stress factors. In this study, (1) an Long Short-Term Memory-Residual Network-Diffusion model with excellent performance is constructed. The model achieves a Mean Absolute Error of 0.28, Root Mean Squared Error of 0.47, Coefficient of Determination of 0.87, and probability value is less than 0.01. (2) Through SHapley Additive exPlanations analysis, the dynamic variation of the driving forces is clarified. As the welding process proceeds, the stress driving force changes from slope, axial stress, and deflection angle to welding torch deflection angle alone. (3) The dynamic variation and critical thresholds of the inhibitory forces are established. The main inhibitory forces for asymmetry stress factors are swing width (0 mm- 3.9 mm), edge dwell time (2.5 s- 8.06 s), and welding speed (14.7 mm/s- 15.9 mm/s).

title: Op-Ed: SeLFIES / TRUMP Bonds: Retirement Security for All
affiliations: Georgetown University - McDonough School of Business and Risktyle

detail.title: Op-Ed: SeLFIES / TRUMP Bonds: Retirement Security for All
detail.abstract: The structural shift in demand for long-duration U.S. Treasury securities-particularly the transition from defined benefit (DB) to defined contribution (DC) pension systems presents both a funding challenge and an opportunity for innovation. As traditional liability-driven investors reduce their footprint, Treasury must increasingly rely on more price-sensitive buyers to absorb duration. At the same time, millions of Americans lack adequate access to retirement savings vehicles. A single innovation can address both challenges. We propose that the United States Treasury introduce SeLFIES (Standard-of-Living-indexed, Forward-starting, Income-only Securities)-branded as TRUMP Bonds (Trusted Retirement Under My President Bonds). Properly implemented, such instruments could deepen structurally stable household demand for long-term Treasuries while strengthening retirement security-including for the uncovered and self-employed.

title: Spatial Sorting and the Geography of Innovation
affiliations: ESE Business School

detail.title: Spatial Sorting and the Geography of Innovation
detail.abstract: The scarce input in the production of new ideas is human cognitive time. Because complex problem solving depends on communication, coordination, and tacit knowledge exchange, the allocation of this time is inherently spatial-and the geographic organization of talent is therefore a first-order determinant of innovation. This paper studies how technologies that increase effective cognitive capacity, most notably artificial intelligence, reshape the spatial equilibrium of innovation. I develop and estimate a spatial equilibrium model in which heterogeneous firms and workers sort across cities while competing for scarce talent and urban space. Complementarities between worker skill and firm problem complexity generate self-reinforcing composition effects, and the framework recovers the full distributions of firm and worker types across cities, allowing technological change to affect the upper tail of economic activity rather than only average productivity. Estimated on a panel of the 50 largest U.S. metropolitan areas from 2019 to 2023, the model matches key cross-city patterns in wages, rents, and sorting. Counterfactuals show that increases in cognitive efficiency primarily reallocate innovative activity rather than scale it uniformly: top workers and complex firms concentrate further in cities with dense complementary networks. Technological progress therefore raises aggregate productivity while simultaneously intensifying the spatial concentration of frontier innovation.

title: AI and Higher Education Job Quality Premiums: Amplification or Levelling?
affiliations: University of Warwick and University College London

detail.title: AI and Higher Education Job Quality Premiums: Amplification or Levelling?
detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of AI across European workplaces raises pressing questions about educational inequality. Whilst graduate wage premiums are well-established, whether AI amplifies or levels graduate advantages across multiple dimensions of job quality remains unknown. Drawing upon the 2024 European Working Conditions Survey, the large-scale European dataset with explicit AI usage measures, we examine how AI interacts with graduate status across seven job quality dimensions among 36,644 workers in 35 countries. Our findings reveal that neither the amplification nor the levelling hypothesis alone characterises AI’s distributional consequences. AI amplifies graduate advantages in Earnings and Social Environment whilst compressing graduate premiums in Skills and Discretion and Prospects. A further stratification emerges in Work Intensity: non-graduates using AI face sharply elevated work demands whilst graduates are largely buffered. The overall pattern is not a simple redistribution of pre-existing advantage but a dimensional restructuring of educational stratification, one that wage-only analyses systematically obscure.

title: Evaluating India's Steel Products Competitiveness with FTA Partners: An Application of Selected Trade Tools
affiliations: Centre for Development Economics and Indian Institute of Foreign Trade (IIFT)

detail.title: Evaluating India's Steel Products Competitiveness with FTA Partners: An Application of Selected Trade Tools
detail.abstract: This paper evaluates India's crude steel competitiveness against major Asian partners (Japan, Korea, ASEAN) from 2001-2020. It analyses how Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) interact with structural capabilities and Global Value Chain (GVC) linkages. Results show Japan, Korea, and China consistently dominate, possessing greater breadth and technological sophistication in their product structures. They exhibit stronger trade complementarity with India, more diversified export baskets, and achieve simultaneous gains in market share and unit values. Conversely, India's exports expand in narrow segments, competing primarily on price rather than quality. Trade in Value-Added (TiVA) data confirms India remains a downstream user of imported metals. Consequently, FTA tariff preferences alone have been insufficient to overcome India's structural disadvantages in product mix, demand alignment, quality, and GVC positioning.

title: Malpractice without a Baseline: Tort Liability and the Structural Paradoxes of Psychedelic-assisted Therapy
affiliations: The Palmieri Law Firm

detail.title: Malpractice without a Baseline: Tort Liability and the Structural Paradoxes of Psychedelic-assisted Therapy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This article is a work of legal scholarship and does not involve human participants, clinical data, or experimental research. Institutional review board approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Psychedelic-assisted therapy is advancing rapidly toward clinical legitimacy in the United States. The Food and Drug Administration has granted Breakthrough Therapy designations to psilocybin and MDMA, several states have established regulated access frameworks, and major research institutions have invested hundreds of millions of dollars in psychedelic science. Yet the legal infrastructure governing malpractice liability for this emerging treatment modality remains almost entirely undeveloped. This Article identifies three structural challenges that psychedelicassisted therapy poses for traditional malpractice doctrine. First, the standard-of-care inquiry confronts an emerging profession that lacks settled credentialing, licensing norms, and practice standards, making expert testimony unreliable and the custom-based standard largely indeterminate. Second, causation analysis breaks down when the treatment intentionally alters the patient's evaluative framework-the cognitive architecture through which the patient assesses whether an outcome constitutes harm. Third, the damages calculus faces a paradox when the alleged injury is identity transformation that the patient may, after the shift, regard as beneficial. This Article argues that these are not transitional problems that will resolve as the field matures; they are structural features of a therapy that deliberately modifies the baseline against which malpractice doctrine measures deviation, causation, and harm. The Article proposes doctrinal adaptations-including prospective consent architectures, tiered standard-of-care frameworks, and temporal damages models-that would allow tort law to govern psychedelic therapy without collapsing the doctrinal coherence that makes malpractice liability meaningful.

title: The Impossibility of Institutional Memory under Decentralized Fairness
affiliations: Friedrich Schiller University - Faculty of Mathematics and Computer Science

detail.title: The Impossibility of Institutional Memory under Decentralized Fairness
detail.abstract: Can decentralized institutions use their own history to stabilize collective decisions? This paper studies dynamic admissibility systems in which a public record of accepted alternatives is updated using decentralized reports from agents. We impose a set of structural principles capturing decentralized fairness: feasibility with respect to current support, independence across alternatives, anonymity across agents, neutrality across alternatives, and non-degeneracy. Together with Minimalist Inheritance and a dynamic richness condition on acceptance paths, these principles determine the informational structure of the resulting admissibility regime. Our main result shows that such systems necessarily generate structurally blind information regimes: along admissible continuation paths, interior support for any alternative can be punctured at arbitrarily late dates. Thus decentralized admissibility systems satisfying these principles cannot build informational mechanisms capable of shielding accepted alternatives from late support erosion. The analysis establishes an institutional trilemma: decentralized fairness and agent agency are fundamentally incompatible with institutional persistence. Institutions that successfully stabilize collective judgments must therefore depart from at least one of these principles.

title: The Governance of Administrative Documents in Cameroon's Public Service: Balancing Transparency, Workflow Efficiency, and Information Security
affiliations: Highstone International University and Highstone International University

detail.title: The Governance of Administrative Documents in Cameroon's Public Service: Balancing Transparency, Workflow Efficiency, and Information Security
detail.abstract: The governance of administrative documents is a central element of modern public administration, influencing transparency, administrative efficiency, and public trust in government institutions. In Cameroon, the increasing digitization of administrative processes has significantly transformed the management, circulation, and preservation of official documents within the public service. This article analyzes the governance of administrative documents in Cameroon through the analytical framework of three interdependent objectives: transparency in citizens' access to administrative information, efficiency in document processing workflows, and protection of document integrity and information security. The study situates document governance within Cameroon's evolving legal and institutional framework, including Prime Ministerial circulars regulating administrative correspondence, the regulatory regime created by Law No. 2010/012 of 21 December 2010 relating to Cybersecurity and Cybercriminality, and criminal law provisions contained in Law No. 2016/007 of 12 July 2016 instituting the Penal Code. The analysis further examines the institutional role of the National Agency for Information and Communication Technologies (ANTIC) in strengthening cybersecurity, digital certification, and electronic document authentication within public administration, including its recent Doc@uthANTIC digital signature initiative designed to combat document forgery and certify the authenticity of official documents. Using qualitative policy analysis and institutional case studies, the article examines key administrative information systems including the evolution from "ANTILOPE" to the Integrated Computerised State Personnel and Payroll Management System (SIGIPES) and the newly introduced "AIGLES" programme, the COLEPS electronic public procurement platform, and the digitization of civil registration and identity documentation processes. Drawing on the doctoral research of Mela (2022), which provides an in-depth sociological analysis of SIGIPES from its conception to appropriation by end-users, the article reveals how these digital tools have been negotiated, adapted, and sometimes circumvented by different categories of actors within the state apparatus. While digital initiatives have improved transparency and administrative efficiency, persistent challenges remain, including infrastructure constraints, coexistence of physical and digital records, limited digital competencies within segments of the public administration, weak enforcement of existing legal frameworks, and the absence of a comprehensive freedom of information law. The study argues that effective governance of administrative documents requires an integrated framework combining legal safeguards, digital technologies, administrative capacity building, and institutional culture reforms. Drawing on recent scholarship on egovernance and local development in Cameroon and emerging research on intelligent architectural frameworks for municipal services , the article proposes strategic recommendations for strengthening Cameroon's administrative document governance. By strengthening these dimensions simultaneously, Cameroon can enhance administrative accountability, improve service delivery efficiency, and protect the integrity of public information systems.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a deductive framework linking micro price formation to the macro price level. We derive a macro distributive equilibrium equation, P = W + Π, showing that price levels fundamentally reflect the distribution of social value between wages and profits. We identify two drivers of price dynamics: structural displacement (natural inflation) and clearing constraints between Consumption Money Flow (MC) and nominal consumption (P×Y). Price changes are decomposed as ΔP = ΔPn+ ΔPc, where ΔPn represents structural shifts and ΔPc reflects clearing ratio deviations. This analysis reveals a systematic purchasing power gap inherent in market economies. The framework implies that stabilization should prioritize aligning MC with P×Y before addressing structural inflationary sources. By clarifying the relationship between price formation and realization, this study provides a unified theory for understanding the structural mechanisms of inflation and deflation.

title: Income Inequality and Campaign Contributions: Evidence from the 1986 Reagan Tax Cut

detail.title: Income Inequality and Campaign Contributions: Evidence from the 1986 Reagan Tax Cut
detail.abstract: Does higher income inequality increase political inequality by raising the political influence of rich donors? We attempt to answer this question by providing evidence of the effects of a policy-induced rise in income inequality on the concentration of campaign contributions in the US. Using a novel dataset at the Census tract level we show that the 1986 Tax Reform Act, which disproportionately benefited wealthy taxpayers, caused a spike in individual contributions, predominantly from donors at the top of the income distribution. The effect was similar for both parties and unrelated to the recipients' ideology or office sought. For members of Congress, the effect was larger for legislators that voted in favour of the tax bill and for candidates likely to be well-connected or from privileged backgrounds. We also find that an increase in disposable income is more likely to induce political donations when the donor and the recipient share a similar social background. Taken together, our results suggest that the effects of tax policy extend beyond the economic domain, with implications for the distribution of political influence through campaign contributions.

detail.abstract: This study examines the role of tourism specialisation in regional economic convergence across Europe between 2003 and 2021 through a conditional β-convergence model estimated at the NUTS 3 level, representing a methodological innovation with respect to previous literature. The results reveal the existence of significant convergence, although with notable differences between nominal and real indicators, the latter showing a slower and more heterogeneous process across regions. Tourism emerges as a positive but non-linear determinant of economic growth, with favourable effects in moderately specialised regions and diminishing-or even adverse-returns in those highly dependent on the sector. In contrast, high-tech industries, knowledge-intensive services, and manufacturing activities display stronger and more stable contributions to convergence, suggesting that technological and productive specialisation fosters long-term resilience and sustained productivity gains. Overall, the findings highlight the need for policies that promote balanced, diversified, and sustainable tourism development capable of effectively contributing to regional cohesion in Europe.

detail.abstract:
Objective: To estimate the economic and social value of potential reforms to the Healthy Start Scheme (HSS) in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and to compare alternative policy scenarios. 

Method: Exploratory cost-benefit analysis (CBA) modelling three policy reforms: (i) increasing voucher value, (ii) introducing auto-enrolment, and (iii) expanding eligibility to households receiving Universal Credit. Benefits included reductions in food insecurity, wider economic effects and household income transfers. Costs included programme expenditure and administration. Outcomes were expressed as net present value (NPV) and benefit cost ratios (BCRs) over 10-and 20-year horizons. Setting: England, Wales and Northern Ireland Participants: Pregnant women and families with young children eligible for, or potentially eligible for, HSS under alternative reform scenarios. 

Results: All reforms generated positive NPVs relative to current policy. Over 10 years, expanding eligibility to Universal Credit produced the largest total social gains (NPV ~ £6.9 billion), while auto-enrolment achieved the highest BCR (~2.45), reflecting improved take-up among already eligible households. Increasing voucher value also generated net benefits, though of smaller magnitude. Results were consistent under a 20-year time horizon. However, estimates were sensitive to assumptions regarding take-up rates, the valuation of food security, and wider economic multiplier effects. 

Conclusions: Reforming the HSS is likely to generate net social benefits, with different reforms offering distinct trade-offs between total impact and efficiency. This analysis adds economic evidence to the public health nutrition debate, suggesting that policy discussions should consider not only nutritional adequacy and equity, but also the broader social value of alternative design choices. Improved causal and valuation evidence would strengthen future economic appraisals of early-years nutrition policies.

detail.abstract: Effective policy design to hasten universal adoption of modern energy sources requires measurement and tracking tools that can capture the multidimensional nature of energy access and transitions. We advance this goal by first reviewing the existing energy access measurement and transition methodologies in literature and assessing their suitability for informing policy design. Our review reveals that current methodologies are unequipped to capture the multidimensional nature of energy access and transitions in the required resolution from publicly available government-generated data. To overcome this issue, we propose a framework combining two methods developed by the authors: the Hierarchical Energy Access Framework (HEAF) and the Household Energy Access Transition (HEAT)-cooking model. We then demonstrate the utility of this framework by analysing energy transitions of rural Indian households between 2011 and 2031. First, we examine the energy access gains made by households between 2011 and 2021. We then devise policies that can improve adoption of modern cooking fuels by 2031. Our analysis indicates that subsidy-based policies alone are unlikely to transition households in the lowest two expenditure-based quintiles to modern fuels by 2031. Instead, policies that enable fuel use for households’ productive aspirations with income and employment generation potential hold greater promise.

title: The Network State Paradox: Governance Innovation, the Limits of Exit, and What the Evidence Actually Supports
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania

detail.title: The Network State Paradox: Governance Innovation, the Limits of Exit, and What the Evidence Actually Supports
detail.abstract: In October 2024, a project called Praxis Nation announced $525 million in financing to build the world's first "network state" — a digital-first community with the expressed aim of acquiring physical territory, escaping existing regulatory frameworks, and "restoring Western Civilization." This paper examines the network state model across ten analytical dimensions: the historical record of utopian community experiments; the ideological framework of The Sovereign Individual (Davidson & Rees-Mogg, 1997); Elinor Ostrom's Nobel Prize-winning research on polycentric governance; the empirical literature on Special Economic Zone success and failure; succession and intergenerational governance problems; questions of inclusion and cultural blind spots; the philosophy of land and ecological obligation; and the civilisational stakes of success rather than failure. The central finding is that the most serious problem with the network state model is not that it will fail, but that it might succeed. Exit by the most capable actors from collective obligations is individually rational and systemically catastrophic, particularly for coordination problems — climate change, pandemic preparedness, nuclear governance, compounding inequality — that require collective action at precisely the scale from which network states are designed to withdraw. The paper concludes by articulating five evidence-grounded principles for governance innovation that address the legitimate acceleration agenda without the systemic costs of the exit model.

title: Rounding of Internal Performance Targets: Determinants and Implications
affiliations: Erasmus University Rotterdam - Erasmus School of Economics, Hong Kong Polytechnic University - School of Accounting and Finance, University of California, Riverside and Hong Kong Polytechnic University

detail.title: Rounding of Internal Performance Targets: Determinants and Implications
detail.abstract: We examine rounding in earnings-per-share (EPS) performance targets used in CEO bonus plans, defined as placing a zero or five in the penny digit. About 42.8% of EPS targets are rounded, more than double the unconditional expected rate of 20%. Rounding is more prevalent when information uncertainty is higher and when compensation committees are more co-opted. Consistent with greater information uncertainty, firms with rounded targets are more likely to issue rounded management forecasts, issue forecasts later, and provide forecasts that are less accurate, more conservative, wider in range, and less informative to the stock market. These firms also make less capital investment, engage in fewer acquisitions, issue less debt, and hold more cash. Finally, CEOs receive higher compensation when EPS targets are rounded, after controlling for performance and firm characteristics. Rounded EPS targets are easier than non-rounded ones to achieve relative to realized EPS, likely facilitating higher compensation payouts. Overall, we provide new evidence on the design of earnings performance targets, which play a central role in incentivizing managers and coordinating firm activities.

detail.abstract: The study endeavours to investigate macroeconomic determinants of exchange rate misalignment in developing countries with a particular emphasis on exchange rate flexibility and capital account openness. At the first stage, the Behavioural Equilibrium Exchange Rate approach has been adopted to compute exchange rate misalignment by estimating the real exchange rate model using the Cross-Sectionally Augmented Autoregressive Distributed Lags technique. In the second stage, the study employs alternative econometric techniques, namely, Pooled Mean Group, Mean Group, and Dynamic Fixed Effects, to assess the drivers of exchange rate misalignment. The empirical results show that both exchange rate flexibility and capital account openness effectively reduce RER misalignment in developing, emerging, and non-emerging economies, through different channels. RER flexibility enables market-adjusted changes, and capital account openness achieves long-run allocative efficiency through connecting the domestic market with global financial flow. Moreover, macroeconomic variables such as GDP growth, inflation, financial sector development, natural resource rents, and foreign direct investment are found to be major drivers of exchange rate misalignment in these countries. Overall, the analysis underlines the need for coherent policy coordination, focusing on capital account liberalization and a flexible exchange rate regime for managing exchange rate misalignment.

detail.abstract: This study examines how rising trade policy uncertainty (TPU) mainly from the US-China trade war affected innovation at Chinese listed firms between 2015 and 2023. Using an industry level TPU index, we measure innovation quantity by patent applications and innovation quality by citation counts. Our results show that rising TPU is positively associated with both the number and the impact of patents, suggesting that uncertainty tends to drive firms toward more and higher-quality innovation. The heterogeneity analysis further indicates that higher TPU exposure is associated with greater innovation activity among small and medium-sized companies, non-state-owned enterprises, and inland companies. By combining firm-level panel data with a novel TPU measure and distinguishing between innovation quantity and quality, this research offers actionable insights for managers allocating R&D resources under uncertainty and for policymakers aiming to stimulate technological progress in volatile trade environments.

title: Economic Statecraft and Political Question: Why the Court used the Wrong Doctrine
affiliations: University of Turin - Faculty of Law, SciencesPo, Ecole de Droit

detail.title: Economic Statecraft and Political Question: Why the Court used the Wrong Doctrine
detail.abstract:
This Article argues that the Supreme Court used the wrong doctrine to decide Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, its recent case invalidating “emergency tariffs.” By allowing judicial review over core instruments of economic foreign policy, the Court ignores the logic of the political question doctrine. The Court treated the dispute as a textbook major questions case.

The deeper question, however, is not how to read IEEPA, but who should decide whether a President may use emergency tariffs as a tool of economic statecraft—shaping negotiations with other states and reallocating economic costs across domestic sectors. Asking courts to arbitrate these choices pushes them beyond ordinary legal interpretation into institutional design. In such cases, the major questions doctrine answers the wrong question.

The Article therefore proposes a simple conceptual clarification. The major questions doctrine addresses how courts should read statutes once they intervene; the political question doctrine addresses the prior institutional question of whether courts should intervene at all. In disputes involving economic statecraft, that threshold question should come first.

detail.abstract: The effects of climate-related disasters hold a syndemic or multiplicative effect on exacerbating pre-existing social epidemics of gender-based violence against women (GBVAW). With increasing patterns in severity and frequency of rapid-onset climate-related disasters anticipated to worsen due to climate change, GBVAW poses a serious threat to exacerbating women's socioeconomic and health disparities. However, limited literature exists that synthesizes understanding of factors that shape women's vulnerability to gender-based violence in relation to rapid-onset climaterelated disasters. In this paper, we aim to identify key factors that shape women's vulnerability to gender-based violence induced by rapid-onset natural disasters through the use of a scoping literature review. Using content analysis, ten key factors were found to shape women's vulnerability to GBVAW through the syndemic effects of rapid-onset climate-related disasters including: 1) preexisting gender inequalities, 2) rigid gendered roles and labor, 3) overwhelmed systemic infrastructure capacity, 4) displacement, 5) loss of social network and social capital, 6) cyclical poverty traps, 7) water and food insecurity, 8) gendered stereotype depictions of women in mass communication, 9) male-centered disaster relief efforts, and 10) weathering conditions to women's health. Based on the key factors identified, the current state of existing literature and gaps in integrating mitigation of GBVAW within climate risk management frameworks are discussed, as well as recent legal pathways and remedies that may support the mitigation of GBVAW in times of rapid-onset climate-related disasters.

title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of GPT Models for Clinical Text Classification Using Electronic Health Record Data
affiliations: California State University Fullerton and University of North Texas

detail.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of GPT Models for Clinical Text Classification Using Electronic Health Record Data
detail.abstract: The increasing availability of unstructured clinical narratives in electronic health records (EHRs) has created new opportunities for automated disease characterization, cohort identification, and clinical decision support. However, effectively modeling long, domain-specific clinical text remains challenging due to limited labeled data, substantial class imbalance, and the high computational cost associated with adapting large pretrained language models to downstream tasks. In this study, a GPT-based architecture for clinical text classification is presented, which adapts a pretrained decoder-only Transformer to downstream clinical tasks using a selective finetuning strategy. Instead of updating all model parameters, the majority of the pretrained GPT-2 backbone is frozen, and training is restricted to the final Transformer block, the final layer normalization, and a lightweight classification head. This design significantly reduces the number of trainable parameters while preserving the representational capacity required for modeling complex clinical language. It evaluates the proposed approach on radiology re-ports from the MIMIC-IV-Note dataset using uncertainty-aware CheXpert-style labels derived directly from report text. Experiments are conducted across multiple problem formulations, including multi-label classification of radiographic findings, binary per-label classification under different uncertainty assumptions, and aggregate disease outcome prediction. Across varying sample sizes, the model demonstrates stable convergence behavior and strong classification performance, particularly in multi-class settings where non-mention and negated findings are prevalent. Overall, the results suggest that selective fine-tuning of pretrained generative language models offers an efficient and effective pathway for clinical text classification, enabling scalable adaptation to real-world EHR data while substantially reducing computational complexity.
