detail.abstract: This paper aims to model user expectations as predictors of continuance intentions of mHealth with community health workers (CHWs) in Malawi, a developing country context. The study extends the expectation confirmation model to include effort expectancy, and quality triads (system quality, information quality, and service quality). A survey questionnaire was used to collect data from 176 randomly sampled CHWs in three district health facilities in Malawi. Partial least squares method to structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyse data. The study found that effort expectancy, confirmation, satisfaction, and post-usage usefulness had a significant influence on CHWs' continuance usage intentions with mHealth in Malawi. However, the unexpected results were that quality triads did not yield positive effects on the continued usage intentions of CHWs with mHealth. This was contrary to the established IS extant literature. The study concludes by making recommendations for policy and research practice.

title: Effective Personalized AI Tutors via LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania, National Taiwan University - Department of Information Management, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and University of Pennsylvania - Department of Computer and Information Science

detail.title: Effective Personalized AI Tutors via LLM-Guided Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping education by unlocking the potential for personalized tutoring. Yet, emerging platforms largely focus on GenAI chatbot tutors that reactively answer student questions. We hypothesize that the efficacy of GenAI chatbot tutors can be substantially improved by proactively guiding student learning. To test this, we design a novel tutoring platform that tightly integrates a carefully-designed GenAI chatbot with a reinforcement learning algorithm for sequencing practice problems. Critically, this algorithm  leverages rich signals from student-chatbot interactions to adaptively select practice problems of an appropriate difficulty level. In partnership with the Taipei City Government and American Institute in Taiwan, we deployed our tutoring platform in conjunction with a five-month course to teach Python to students across ten high schools. We randomized students between a fixed practice problem sequence and our adaptive sequencing algorithm. We find that adaptive sequencing increased unassisted final exam performance by 0.15 standard deviations (equivalent to 6-9 months of schooling by some estimates); mediation analysis suggests that gains were driven by increased engagement. Our work provides large-scale field evidence that student-chatbot interactions provide valuable signals for proactively optimizing and personalizing student learning.

title: Revisiting Sovereign Authority & International Order: A Game-Theoretic Hypothesis on Structural Trust Equilibrium
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Revisiting Sovereign Authority & International Order: A Game-Theoretic Hypothesis on Structural Trust Equilibrium
detail.abstract:
This article uses three contemporary geopolitical episodes; 

• the January 2026 capture of Venezuela's sitting president by United States forces, 
• the escalation of open conflict following pre-emptive strikes involving the United States, Israel, and Iran, and 
• the International Court of Justice's 2025 advisory opinion on climate change obligations 

as practical demonstrations of a deeper structural phenomenon: trust equilibrium. 

Drawing on game-theoretic insights, it hypothesises that sovereign authority and the international order endure not solely by virtue of formal recognition or doctrinal coherence, but because relevant actors maintain convergent expectations that authority will be exercised co-operatively and competently under conditions of uncertainty. 

Where those expectations align, legitimacy stabilises. Where they fragment, authority destabilises. 

By reconceptualising legitimacy as a dynamic equilibrium of co-operative belief, the article offers a descriptive and explanatory account of authority persistence and collapse, and suggests a pathway beyond the enduring indeterminacy of contemporary public international legal theory.

title: Him Too? Analyzing the Effects of Epstein Connections
affiliations: University of Melbourne, Washington University in St. Louis - John M. Olin Business School and University of Melbourne - Faculty of Business and Economics

detail.title: Him Too? Analyzing the Effects of Epstein Connections
detail.abstract:
The Epstein files, released between September 2025 and January 2026, provide an unprecedented view into the social and professional network of a convicted sex offender whose connections reached deep into corporate America. We construct a comprehensive sample of all S&P 500 CEOs and board members serving between 2006 and 2026, comprising 52,266 unique individuals, and search 1,293,753 text-bearing documents for evidence of their contact with Jeffrey Epstein. Using large language model (LLM) classification on 117,394 matched correspondences, we identify 67,637 instances that indicate direct contact involving 1,179 S&P 500 CEOs or directors.

We document three main findings. First, firms whose CEOs or board members were mentioned in Epstein-related news coverage experienced significantly negative cumulative abnormal returns of up to −3.7% over a three-day window following the Department of Justice release on January 30, 2026. Second, incorporating Epstein-mediated ties into the firm network increases overall density and significantly reduces average path lengths, indicating that Epstein effectively made corporate America more tightly interconnected than it would have been otherwise. Third, we show that Epstein’s network facilitated norm contagion through shared board connections. Firms with more Epstein-connected CEOs or directors exhibit significantly worse ESG outcomes: each additional connection is associated with approximately 2.3 more annual governance incidents and 4.0 more total incidents.

title: Real Options in Pharmaceutical API Network Design: A Critical Review of Evidence, Contradictions, and Unresolved Debates
affiliations: Novo Nordisk

detail.title: Real Options in Pharmaceutical API Network Design: A Critical Review of Evidence, Contradictions, and Unresolved Debates
detail.abstract:
Pharmaceutical active ingredient and upstream manufacturing networks operate under a distinctive mix of long construction lead times, technical and regulatory uncertainty, volatile launch trajectories, and high costs of irreversible capacity commitments. These features make real options logic attractive because investment timing, sourcing configuration, modularity, and multisite design can be interpreted as contingent rights rather than static cost tradeoffs (Kogut and Kulatilaka 1994; Huchzermeier and Cohen 1996; Bengtsson 2001; Mieghem 2003). This review assesses the state of knowledge on whether real options is a useful decision lens for pharmaceutical API and upstream network design. The review synthesizes direct pharma studies on staged capacity investment and flexible launch capacity, broader pharmaceutical network design models under uncertainty, API sourcing and dual-sourcing studies, and general operations literature that provides the conceptual foundation for option-based reasoning (Papageorgiou, Rotstein, and Shah 2001; Levis and Papageorgiou 2004; Chambers, Snir, and Ata 2009; Okajima, Xu, and Zhao 2012; Lindahl, Babi, and Sin 2024; Blossey, Hahn, and Koberstein 2021a). 
The literature is more unified on principle than on prescription. Across streams, flexibility usually creates value under uncertainty, and static net present value or unit cost comparisons often miss economically relevant timing, switching, and recourse effects (Chambers, Snir, and Ata 2009; Kaminsky and Yuen 2014; Okajima, Xu, and Zhao 2012; Bengtsson 2001; Mieghem 2003). However, studies reach different conclusions about the optimal amount of flexible capacity, whether delay dominates early commitment, whether redundancy is worth paying for, and whether explicit real-options models add material value beyond multistage stochastic planning (Hansen and Grunow 2015; Lücker and Seifert 2017; Tucker et al. 2019; Lindahl, Babi, and Sin 2024; Sarkis, Shah, and Papathanasiou 2025b). Most of these contradictions are conditional rather than fundamental. They arise from differences in uncertainty structure, objective function, technology assumptions, and system boundary. The review concludes that the field is mature enough to justify explicit valuation of flexibility in pharmaceutical API network design, but not mature enough to support a universal rule for the best flexibility portfolio across settings (Franco and Alfonso-Lizarazo 2017; Settanni, Harrington, and Srai 2017; Blossey, Hahn, and Koberstein 2021a; Marques et al. 2020).

title: Limits of Executive Power: DACA and the Instability of Immigration Relief
affiliations: South Texas College of Law Houston

detail.title: Limits of Executive Power: DACA and the Instability of Immigration Relief
detail.abstract:
The Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program has provided temporary relief to hundreds of thousands of undocumented individuals brought to the United States as children. However, a decade of litigation, rescission attempts, and shifting executive priorities has exposed a fundamental structural problem that immigration policy created through executive action alone cannot provide durable legal protection. This paper argues that DACA, as an exercise of executive authority independent from congressional authorization, is constitutionally unjustifiable under the framework established in Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, and that its continued instability will persist until Congress acts.

This paper examines DACA through key executive actions and litigation, including its creation through Department of Homeland Security memorandum, subsequent rescission efforts, and a series of judicial decisions that have shaped its current form. It demonstrates that courts have addressed challenges to DACA on procedural grounds but consistently avoid answering the program’s underlying issue about constitutional validity. As a result, DACA remains neither legislatively authorized nor definitively upheld by courts, existing within a legally contested space. 

Furthermore, the paper examines the real-world consequences of this instability, focusing on the reliance interests of recipients whose education, employment, and long-term planning depend on the program’s continued existence. Specifically, its impact on graduate and postgraduate students, whose professional pathways require sustained legal and economic stability. Using Texas as a case study to demonstrate how, in the absence of federal certainty, state regulatory frameworks can create indirect but significant structural pressures on DACA recipients that may effectively compel relocation.

Ultimately, this paper contends that executive action cannot serve as a durable substitute for legislative reform. Absent congressional intervention, DACA will remain a temporary and constitutionally unjustifiable solution, leaving its recipients in a persistent state of legal and economic uncertainty.

title: An Option Pricing Framework for Valuation of Football Players: Transfer Windows and Release Clauses
affiliations: Tokyo University of Science, Tokyo University of Science - Department of Industrial Administration, Cerezo Osaka Co., Ltd, Cerezo Osaka Co., Ltd, Yanmar Holdings Co., Ltd, Yanmar Holdings Co., Ltd, Yanmar Holdings Co., Ltd, Yanmar Holdings Co., Ltd and Yanmar Holdings Co., Ltd

detail.title: An Option Pricing Framework for Valuation of Football Players: Transfer Windows and Release Clauses
detail.abstract: This study develops a dynamic framework for evaluating professional football player contracts under institutional trading constraints. We incorporate transfer windows and release clauses, which restrict when transfers can occur and under what terms. Player performance is represented by a stochastic process based on a revenueadjusted Opta metric, and the club's decision problem is formulated with time-dependent constraints. Numerical analysis reveals two main mechanisms. First, under realistic market conditions, voluntary sellouts are not optimal ("rational retention"). As contract expiration approaches, the declining remaining duration expands the set of situations in which accepting a transfer becomes optimal, generating a pronounced deadline effect. Second, release clauses reduce the club's discretion by making highperforming players harder to retain when interest from other clubs arrives. Sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting cost is particularly large for rapidly developing players and in high-liquidity markets with frequent transfer offers, while it is less affected by downside risks such as injuries. An empirical application using proprietary data from a J.League club shows that incorporating these institutional features changes contract evaluations materially, yields a lower bound tied to the release fee relative to a static DCF benchmark, and confirms through counterfactual experiments that the deadline effect is driven by horizon contraction rather than short-term performance fluctuations.

title: Which Taylor Rule Variant Best Predicted U.S. Inflation? An Empirical Analysis of Monetary Policy Gaps, 2019-2025

detail.title: Which Taylor Rule Variant Best Predicted U.S. Inflation? An Empirical Analysis of Monetary Policy Gaps, 2019-2025
detail.abstract: This paper provides an ex-post empirical evaluation of three Taylor Rule variants, specifically the Original Taylor (1993) rule, the Balanced Approach Rule, and the Inertial Taylor Rule, as leading indicators of U.S. core PCE inflation over January 2019 through December 2025. Using monthly FRED data, we compute the policy gap for each rule and test its association with realized inflation at six-and twelve-month horizons. All regressions employ Newey-West HAC standard errors to correct for the serial correlation induced by overlapping forecast horizons. We report two sets of controlled regressions: one using the NY Fed Global Supply Chain Pressure Index (GSCPI) as a supply shock proxy (Table 3a), and one adding the federal deficit as a share of GDP as a fiscal control (Table 3b). We also conduct a subsample analysis separating the pre-COVID period from the post-lockdown recovery. In the baseline specification, the Original Taylor (1993) rule produces the highest predictive accuracy at both horizons (R² = 0.763 at t+6; R² = 0.444 at t+12), ranking above the Balanced Approach (R² = 0.725; 0.318) and Inertial Taylor Rule (R² = 0.684; 0.305). This ranking is robust to HAC standard errors, supply-side and fiscal controls, a lagged gap predictor, and sensitivity analysis over the neutral rate r* ∈ {0%, 0.5%, 1%, 2%}. The subsample analysis reveals that the Original Taylor Rule holds its full-sample advantage when the entire 2019 to 2025 period is considered; results from the short pre-COVID window (n = 14) are inconclusive due to insufficient statistical power, and the Balanced Approach edges out the Original Taylor in the post-lockdown period alone (R² = 0.889 versus 0.875). A secondary finding is that predictive power decays sharply between the six-and twelve-month horizons across all rules, consistent with monetary policy transmission lags. These results are ex-post in nature and should be interpreted as characterizing which rule provided the strongest retrospective inflation signal over this specific episode, not as evidence of structural superiority across all macroeconomic environments.

title: AI Investments and Female Participation in Innovation Activities
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE) - Chinese Academy of Finance and Development, Hong Kong Polytechnic University,  and Nanjing University - School of Business

detail.title: AI Investments and Female Participation in Innovation Activities
detail.abstract: Women remain severely underrepresented among patent inventors despite policy efforts and workforce diversification initiatives. Whether firm-level artificial intelligence (AI) investments exacerbate or alleviate this gap is an open and consequential question. This study examines the relationship between firm-level AI investments and female participation in corporate innovation activities. Using a panel of U.S. public firms from 2010 to 2021, we find a positive association between AI investments and the share of women inventors. Further analysis shows that this relationship is explained by reduced gender productivity gaps, enhanced female career advancement, and improved cross-gender collaboration. Moreover, leveraging the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) as a policy shock that limits the potential for algorithmic bias among U.S. firms with EU exposure, we find that the positive effect of AI on female participation in innovation is significantly strengthened in the post-implementation period. Heterogeneity analyses show that the gendered effect is stronger for AI applications in science, engineering, and operations; for AI usage by rank-and-file employees; and for firms located in Democratic-leaning states. Furthermore, we document that the AI-driven increase in female participation generates positive real effects. At the firm level, the gendered effect is associated with higher firm valuation, improved operating and innovation performance, and a strategic shift toward exploitative and process-oriented innovation. At the team level, the gendered effect enhances collaborative productivity in research teams-particularly those including disadvantaged female inventors. Our findings underscore how AI can foster gender equity in high-skill labor markets, providing empirical support for the view that AI can serve as a tool for mitigating the participation gap between socioeconomically advantaged and disadvantaged groups.

title: Bionic-Optimized Deep Residual Networks for Enhanced Delineation of Medical Imagery
affiliations: Fuzhou University of International Studies and Trade, Fuzhou University, Fuzhou University of International Studies and Trade and Northwestern Polytechnical University

detail.title: Bionic-Optimized Deep Residual Networks for Enhanced Delineation of Medical Imagery
detail.abstract: To address the challenges of hyperparameter sensitivity and loss of fine details in medical image segmentation, particularly in pneumonia lesion analysis, this study introduces a novel neural network architecture named UNet-ResNet50-ACO. The proposed framework integrates the Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) algorithm with a deep residual U-Net. The ACO component establishes a dynamic parameter optimization mechanism through efficient bio-inspired global search, enabling automated hyperparameter tuning. Simultaneously, residual skip connections within the encoder enhance feature propagation and mitigate network degradation, thereby improving the perception of subtle lesion features. Evaluated on the COVID-19 Radiography Dataset, the method achieves a Dice coefficient of 97.36\%, representing an improvement of approximately 18 percentage points over the standard U-Net baseline, along with concurrent gains in IoU and mIoU. Ablation studies confirm the individual contributions of both the ResNet50 backbone and the ACO algorithm. Moreover, the model demonstrates robust contour recognition capabilities under low-contrast imaging conditions. The main contributions of this work are: (1) a collaborative ACO-CNN mechanism for intelligent hyperparameter space exploration; (2) suppression of semantic attenuation through the integration of residual learning and the U-Net architecture; and (3) a modular and highly adaptable framework for multimodal medical image analysis, offering a practical solution for intelligent pulmonary disease diagnosis.

title: A Novel Markov Model for On-demand Meal Delivery
affiliations: , The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney, The University of Sydney and Zhejiang University

detail.title: A Novel Markov Model for On-demand Meal Delivery
detail.abstract: On-demand meal delivery systems involve continuous spatial interactions between kitchens, customers, and couriers, giving rise to complex network dynamics that are difficult to characterise analytically. This study develops a Markov network model that represents courier movements as probabilistic transitions between spatial nodes, enabling the steadystate structure of delivery activity to be explicitly analysed. Transition probabilities are derived using a maximum entropy formulation subject to delivery-time constraints. The time sensitivity parameter is estimated by maximum likelihood estimation using large-scale operational data from the Meituan delivery platform. The calibrated model produces a stationary distribution representing the steady-state equilibrium of the delivery network, capturing spatial demand attraction and delivery flow patterns across the system. Kitchen relocation experiments are conducted to examine how spatial positioning affects steady-state system performance. The results show that relocation induces systematic changes in kitchen visit probability and average delivery time, revealing spatial trade-offs between demand attraction and delivery efficiency. These findings demonstrate that the proposed framework provides a tractable and empirically grounded representation of delivery network equilibrium and offers a quantitative basis for evaluating kitchen siting and spatial operational decisions in on-demand delivery systems.

title: Multivariate Analysis of Between- and Within-Athlete Technical Variability During Pole Vault
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, affiliation not provided to SSRN, The University of Western Australia, The University of Western Australia, The University of Western Australia and The University of Western Australia

detail.title: Multivariate Analysis of Between- and Within-Athlete Technical Variability During Pole Vault
detail.abstract: Current literature fails to adequately investigate the complex nature of centre of mass (COM) movement in relation to pole bend mechanics during the flight phase of pole vault. We describe the nature of these related variables as functional time series. Eleven developmental to world-class pole vaulters (7 Female, 5 Male; PB range: 3.60-5.41m) completed 65 pole vault trials. Markerless motion capture extracted joint centre trajectories to derive COM position and pole cord length. Time series were segmented from pole plant to top-hand release; represented using multilevel, multivariate, functional principal component analysis. Two between- and four within-participants modes of variation were identified. Between-participants modes observed variation in both movement and pole bend timing throughout the phase and specifically after maximum pole bend. Within-participant modes showed similar patterns of variation to those found between-participants, with additional observation of variation in pole bend during the critical final portion of the phase. These modes indicate that athletes use multiple movement strategies to regulate pole energy storage and release, demonstrating technical variability within constrained performance outcomes in pole vaulting. We show that functional data can be utilised to comprehensively describe movement during a complicated task while demonstrating potential for future analysis using similar statistical methodology.

title: Governance Failures and Flood Risk in the United States: Diagnosing Institutional Dysfunction at the Science-Policy Interface

detail.title: Governance Failures and Flood Risk in the United States: Diagnosing Institutional Dysfunction at the Science-Policy Interface

detail.abstract: The United States loses more wealth to flooding than any other country, yet the governance architecture responsible for translating scientific flood risk knowledge into policy action has remained structurally impaired for decades. This paper diagnoses the sources of that impairment. Drawing on the comparative flood governance literature, institutional analysis of the National Flood Insurance Program, and documentary review of federal and state regulatory frameworks, the paper identifies four interlocking dysfunctions: the institutionalization of moral hazard through federally subsidized insurance; the failure of flood mapping to reflect current and future hazard conditions; the fragmentation of authority across federal, state, and local levels without effective coordination mechanisms; and the systematic exclusion of scientific evidence from floodplain management regulatory cycles. Each dysfunction is traceable not to ignorance of the problem but to specific governance design choices that have been repeatedly reinforced through legislative and administrative action. The paper proposes four reform principles drawn from governance systems with demonstrated superior flood risk outcomes, arguing that the gap between US scientific Omoyeni, B.T. | Governance Failures and Flood Risk in the US | Working Paper 2026 pg. 2 capacity in flood hazard analysis and US policy performance in flood risk reduction represents not a knowledge failure but a governance failure that is both diagnosable and correctable.

title: Extinction Risk and Conservation under Continuous Management
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice - Dipartimento di Economia

detail.title: Extinction Risk and Conservation under Continuous Management
detail.abstract: This paper studies optimal conservation policy under extinction risk in a stochastic framework where population dynamics are subject to environmental uncertainty and extinction is modeled as an absorbing boundary. Building on the real options approach, we depart from the existing literature by modeling intervention as continuous, state-dependent management rather than as a discrete change in biological parameters. In our framework, a planner can irreversibly switch to a regime that enables continuous control of the population drift at a convex cost, introducing a joint decision over the timing and intensity of intervention. The problem is characterized by coupled variational inequalities and solved numerically. The results show that continuous management fundamentally alters policy design: instead of a simple threshold rule, intervention is concentrated over intermediate population states, where the trade-off between extinction risk and management costs is most pronounced, and conservation policy involves adjusting both when and how intensively to intervene.

title: Waste Accumulation as a Flood Risk Driver at the Local Government Level: Policy Evidence from Ikere Local Government Area, Ekiti State, Nigeria

detail.title: Waste Accumulation as a Flood Risk Driver at the Local Government Level: Policy Evidence from Ikere Local Government Area, Ekiti State, Nigeria
detail.abstract: The relationship between poor waste management and urban flooding is well-established in the Nigerian literature at the metropolitan scale, particularly in studies focused on Lagos, Ibadan, and Kano. What the literature lacks is empirical evidence from the sub-metropolitan level, specifically from the local government area as an operational unit, where the practical management of drains, culverts, and waterways actually takes place. This working paper provides that evidence. Drawing on a technical consultancy conducted for Ikere Local Government Council in Ekiti State, Nigeria, between February and May 2025, and reported formally in August 2025, this paper presents the policy findings from that engagement and situates them within the national and international literature on waste management, drainage governance, and local flood risk reduction. The consultancy involved a rapid field assessment of waste-related conditions across drains, culverts, and waterways in Ikere LGA, identification of priority blockage points, development of waste minimization recommendations, provision of drainage cleanliness guidance, and production of implementation guidance for LGA operational teams. The central argument of this paper is that waste accumulation in drainage infrastructure functions as a structural, not incidental, flood risk driver at the local government level, and that managing this risk requires a governance response, not merely a technical or community awareness one. The field findings from Ikere confirm what the national literature has established in the aggregate: that recurrent blockage is driven by the combination of indiscriminate waste disposal practices, the absence of structured routine monitoring of priority drainage assets, and inadequate reporting and escalation mechanisms that would allow operational teams to address emerging blockage conditions before they mature into flooding events. The paper draws policy implications from the Ikere experience that extend beyond Ekiti State, offering a replicable model for waste minimisation and drainage protection that other Nigerian LGAs can adapt within their existing administrative capacity.

title: Features of Ethiopian Federalism

detail.title: Features of Ethiopian Federalism
detail.abstract: This Chapter examines the defining features of Ethiopia’s post-1995 federal order and situates them within debates on state design, nationalism, and constitutionalism. The chapter identifies a set of distinguishing characteristics—radical recognition of national self-determination, ethnicized territorial governance, group-prioritised constitutional rights, and a hybrid federal–confederal political architecture—and explains how these emerged from Ethiopia’s attempt to manage national diversity after regime collapse. It analyzes the political rationality behind using nationality as the primary unit of state formation and shows how this choice has institutionalized nationalism, reshaped citizenship, and produced a federal system that is politically symmetrical yet administratively and socio-economically asymmetrical. Attention is given to institutional design, including non-judicial constitutional interpretation by the House of Federation, parliamentary government with presidential-level executive powers, uneven population–seat representation in the lower house, party-structured federal–state relations, and two modes of local government formation (self-determination–driven and administratively devolved). The chapter argues that these features have generated a centralised party-state alongside a formally decentralised constitutional order, creating persistent tensions between the rights-based logic of multinational federalism and the control-based logic of dominant-party governance. The chapter concludes that Ethiopian federalism remains a project in motion: it has expanded political participation for nations, nationalities, and peoples, yet it has also produced suspended territorial conflicts, managed self-determination claims, and a fragile equilibrium between secession-enabled constitutional design and unity-oriented state practice. The core scholarly contribution is the demonstration that Ethiopia’s federal experiment cannot be understood through existing models; it represents a distinctive case of federal formation through recognition, in which nationalism is both the problem to be governed and the instrument through which governance occurs.

title: Nondiscrimination As Discrimination: The MFN Obligation And International Trade Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming American Journal of International Law

detail.abstract: There is a widespread sense among international economic lawyers that the most-favored-nation obligation, as the expression of a nondiscrimination norm is fundamental for international trade law. But ought they adorn MFN with its normative halo? This article studies the historical emergence of the MFN-as-fundamental mythology. It shows that this mythology is the outcome of three controversial projects over the course of the twentieth century. Embedded historically, they reveal that much less than nondiscrimination, MFN has historically been the vector for drawing the boundaries across which discrimination operates, whether between imperial powers and colonies, or between the West and the East. It is only out of a relatively recent, and intellectually radical turn that MFN became synonymous with the very idea of a universalist, nondiscrimination-centric, international trade law. But that intellectual universeordoliberalism-now being past us, this Article asks what account can we offer of alternative norms that have structured international trade law.

title: Optimal Containment Policy with Private Protection

detail.title: Optimal Containment Policy with Private Protection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: In this paper, I develop a macro-SIR model to analyze how private protection changes optimal containment policy. Mask-wearing as a form of private protection reduces infection risk without requiring a proportional reduction in economic activity and, when sufficiently effective, qualitatively reshapes the optimal containment path. Optimal containment can be phase-shifted-remaining relatively flat during the infection upswing and tightening as infections decline. Under the benchmark calibration, mask-wearing reduces infections more strongly and causes a smaller recession than containment when each is considered in isolation. Although mask-wearing is effective in suppressing transmission, containment remains welfare-improving because it mitigates the infection externality generated by infected individuals' economic activity.

title: NIMAT-Medical: Non-Intrusive Memory Dependency Injection for Longitudinal Evidence Retrieval in Clinical Transformers ​​
affiliations: University of Technology Sydney (UTS) - Faculty of Engineering and IT and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: NIMAT-Medical: Non-Intrusive Memory Dependency Injection for Longitudinal Evidence Retrieval in Clinical Transformers ​​
detail.abstract: Transformer-based models are powerful clinical language backbones, yet their finite context windows fundamentally limit longitudinal reasoning over pa- tient trajectories that may span years of heterogeneous medical events. We present NIMAT-Medical, a non-intrusive memory-augmented framework that formalizes Memory Dependency Injection (MDI) for clinical decision support. A frozen clinical Transformer encoder retrieves top-k de-identified patient events from a patient-partitioned FAISS vector memory, and the retrieved ev- idence is injected at inference time without modifying backbone weights. We propose two complementary injection pathways: (i) MDI-RAG, a prompt- level augmentation approach offering interpretability through readable evi- dence; and (ii) MDI-Hook, a novel latent attention injection mechanism that projects retrieved evidence embeddings into the backbone’s attention space as virtual prefix keys/values, bypassing prompt-length constraints while pre- serving the frozen backbone. On a fully reproducible synthetic patient- history QA benchmark (test split: 50 patients, 1,429 events, 300 queries), MDI-RAG with Canonical Answer Extraction (CAE) achieves 100% EM/F1 as an engineering upper bound under a pipeline-specific retrieval configu- ration with perfect evidence coverage. In a strictly controlled comparative setting (Baseline Configuration, k = 10, EvidenceHit@10 = 93.33%), MDI- Hook achieves 30.33% token-F1, outperforming the Standard RAG baseline (27.23% token-F1) by +3.10 points. We further provide retrieval depth abla- tions, per-task breakdowns, qualitative failure analysis, and runtime observations. Taken together, the results suggest that inference-time latent memory injection can use retrieved longitudinal evidence more effectively than prompt concatenation while preserving a frozen-backbone, patient-partitioned de- ployment design.

title: Welfare and Strategic Implications of Socioeconomic Disparities in School Choice
affiliations: Bates White Economic Consulting and Washington University in St-Louis

detail.title: Welfare and Strategic Implications of Socioeconomic Disparities in School Choice
detail.abstract: Market design aims to improve equity in resource allocation, yet school choice mechanisms can interact with socioeconomic inequality in ways that undermine this goal. The conventional view is that a merit-based assignment mechanism reproduces inequality because test scores reflect pre-existing gaps in educational investment. This paper argues that any non-strategy-proof mechanism itself also plays a direct role in perpetuating inequality, even when holding prior achievement fixed. Students with better outside options weigh the risk of rejection differently and thus strategically report more ambitious rank-order lists to the assignment mechanism, with more competitive programs listed more frequently and ranked higher. Studying this phenomenon is empirically challenging because submitted rank-order lists conflate true preferences with strategic responses to admission probabilities. We separately identify the utility of a match and the insurance value of outside options by exploiting cohort-level variation in admission probabilities together with student-level characteristics that shift the value of outside alternatives. Using administrative data from a large university in Colombia, we find that socioeconomic gaps in ranking behavior are driven in large part by differences in access to outside options.

title: Context, Perspective, or Argument? Perhaps None! (Introducing the Concept of "Teleotexture" in Hermeneutic Realism)

detail.title: Context, Perspective, or Argument? Perhaps None! (Introducing the Concept of "Teleotexture" in Hermeneutic Realism)

detail.abstract: This paper challenges the triadic dominance of context, perspective, and argument as the ultimate arbiters of validity in epistemological discourse. While contemporary thought often treats 'context' as an inescapable horizon and 'perspective' as the unavoidable filter of truth, this inquiry suggests that such frameworks may inadvertently mask a more fundamental mechanism of intellectual survival. By advancing the 'Evolutionary Pragmatist' stance, the author argues that the reliability of a model does not emerge from the internal consistency of an 'argument' nor from the richness of its 'context,' but from its resilience against failure. If scientific and philosophical progress is defined as a collective departure from error, then the survival of an idea is independent of the justifications we construct for it. The paper posits that beyond the subjective and the contextual lies a domain of 'functional necessity' where ideas are selected not because they are 'argued' to be true, but because they are the only ones left standing after the elimination of the dysfunctional. This shift moves epistemology away from justification-based reasoning toward a survival-based realism.

title: The Familiar Face of Harm: Intimacy, Violence and the Enduring Legacy of Classical Literature

detail.title: The Familiar Face of Harm: Intimacy, Violence and the Enduring Legacy of Classical Literature

detail.abstract: This paper examines violence within intimate and familial relations not as a sequence of isolated acts or individual moral failures, but as a structurally reproducible social mechanism. Drawing on nineteenth-century classical literature, the analysis demonstrates how violence becomes socially compatible through economic dependency, moral rationalization, and the normalization of asymmetrical responsibility. Rather than focusing on extreme or criminally legible forms of harm, the paper reconstructs the conditions under which destruction remains imperceptible and appropriation becomes legitimate. By comparing literary configurations with contemporary social arrangements, the study shows that modern legal and welfare frameworks have modified the visibility of violence without dismantling its underlying structure. Classical literature thus remains analytically relevant not as a historical archive, but as a diagnostic instrument for understanding the persistence of intimate violence in contemporary societies.

detail.abstract: On February 2, 2026, the IBCI launched its annual series of webinars and events, establishing a cross-sector regulatory agenda for the year. The first event focused on legislative proposals intended to regulate digital platforms in Brazil and sought to collect evidence and expert assessments from Brazilian and international specialists. The adoption of these proposals, and the institutional reconfiguration they may entail, could have far-reaching regulatory, economic, and strategic implications for Brazil’s digital governance landscape. As these bills continue to be considered within Brazil’s legislative process, key design choices remain contested. However, there is still no clear convergence around the specific regulatory architecture to be adopted, including the allocation of mandates and enforcement responsibilities. While multiple stakeholders share an interest in legal certainty and effective oversight, perspectives diverge on CADE’s prospective role and on how lessons from European and UK approaches should inform Brazilian rulemaking, alongside industry and Latin American academic experience. Following the webinar convened by the IBCI, participants and organizers consolidated the main points raised during the discussion. Based on these inputs, this report synthesizes the evidence collected and sets out conclusions and recommendations intended to inform Brazil’s ongoing national debate on the regulation of digital platforms and artificial intelligence.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper explores the practical application of legal decision-making strategies in guiding ethical considerations in data harvesting research projects. It is shown that the logic used in legal methodology, namely the identification of case groups based on real cases brought to court, can be used to provide balanced and nuanced responses to ethical problems. This is exemplified via the Nissenbaum paradox, where it is fair to assume that data deserve privacy protection even though they are openly accessible, the Sweeney problem, which relates to the natural limits of anonymization, and the problems and risks of clustering anonymized data and thus defining groups that are unknown a priori. The scope of this research is limited by its focus on European legal frameworks, suggesting further exploration in different global contexts. The research reveals a nuanced balance between individual and public interests, including the interest in the advancement of research. The actionability of the amalgamated methodology for ethics policymakers, ethics committees, and researchers is practically demonstrated in the form of ethics checklists provided within this study.

title: Transformer-based CoVaR: Systemic Risk in Textual Information
affiliations: , University of Groningen, University of Groningen and University of Groningen

detail.title: Transformer-based CoVaR: Systemic Risk in Textual Information
detail.abstract: Conditional Value-at-Risk (CoVaR) quantifies systemic financial risk by measuring the loss quantile of one asset, conditional on another asset experiencing distress. We develop a Transformer-based methodology that integrates financial news articles directly with market data to improve CoVaR estimates. Unlike approaches that use predefined sentiment scores, our method incorporates raw text embeddings generated by a large language model (LLM). We prove explicit error bounds for our Transformer CoVaR estimator, showing that accurate CoVaR learning is possible even with small datasets. Using U.S. market returns and Reuters news items from 2006-2013, our out-of-sample results show that textual information impacts the CoVaR forecasts. With better predictive performance, we identify a pronounced negative dip during market stress periods across several equity assets when comparing the Transformer-based CoVaR to both the CoVaR without text and the CoVaR using traditional sentiment measures. Our results show that textual data can be used to effectively model systemic risk without requiring prohibitively large data sets.

title: Cybersecurity as Capital Allocation: An Exposure-Adjusted Governance Framework for Board-Level Risk Oversight

detail.title: Cybersecurity as Capital Allocation: An Exposure-Adjusted Governance Framework for Board-Level Risk Oversight

detail.abstract:
Cybersecurity spending by organizations worldwide is projected to exceed USD 240 billion by 2026, yet board-level governance of cybersecurity investment remains largely disconnected from the capital allocation frameworks that govern other strategic domains of equivalent financial materiality. This paper argues that the gap is not informational but structural: organizations possess established methodologies for quantifying cyber risk in financial terms, including Annual Loss Expectancy and the Factor Analysis of Information Risk model, but these methodologies have not been integrated into the capital governance processes through which boards allocate constrained resources across competing priorities.

The paper develops a governance framework that bridges this gap through three mechanisms. First, it adapts established risk quantification principles into an Exposure-Adjusted Estimation construct calibrated for board-level comparative judgment rather than actuarial precision. Second, it introduces a Risk Efficiency Ratio that enables prioritization of cybersecurity initiatives using the same marginal return logic applied in capital budgeting, insurance pricing, and portfolio management. Third, it proposes a four-domain portfolio model that categorizes cybersecurity investments by their function in reducing different components of enterprise exposure, enabling boards to assess concentration, balance, and strategic alignment. The framework is contextualized within the regulatory requirements established by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission’s 2023 cybersecurity disclosure rules. Three propositions connecting capital allocation governance to measurable outcomes are derived from the framework. The paper contributes to the cybersecurity economics literature by providing the first structured mechanism for integrating quantitative cyber risk assessment into enterprise capital governance processes.

title: AI Information Equilibria Across Social Niches

detail.title: AI Information Equilibria Across Social Niches

detail.abstract:
In the AI era, the classic openness–secrecy dilemma shifts because information is not exposed only to human competitors and audiences. It is increasingly exposed to models and to training/retrieval infrastructures that absorb, compress, and redistribute patterns at scale. This manuscript formalizes the resulting “information equilibria” across social niches, focusing on practical decisions such as: what to publish, what to keep private, and how to interact with AI systems without losing credit or control.

We propose a payoff decomposition U(s)=V(s)+CA(s)−L(s)+D−G(s), where V(s) is feedback gain, CA(s) is credit accrual (how contributions are recorded and returned), L(s) is leakage risk (including model-mediated redistribution and de-attribution), D is defensibility (black-box, asset/scale, brand resonance, execution density), and G(s) is governance/compliance cost. Using four niche archetypes—enterprise leadership, the scientific community, the tech–empire builder, and the unaffiliated independent researcher (Type D)—we show why rational strategies diverge even when actors share intelligence and ambition: niches weight parameters differently, and different defensibility sources support different layers of openness.

A central contribution is ART (Auditable Reasoning Trail): a mechanism by which Type D can treat openness not merely as feedback-seeking but as credit capture under algorithmic distribution. By publishing an auditable chain of reasoning, revisions, and timestamps, Type D increases the probability of being reliably pointed-to (attributed) rather than merely seen. We conclude with implications and testable predictions, including a polarization tendency toward closed giants and open individuals, and a minimal measurement sketch for empirical examination.

detail.abstract: This paper considers a maintenance scheduling problem on a single machine with a fixed job sequence involving job-dependent, stochastic deterioration. If the machine breaks down, then a time-consuming emergency maintenance activity needs to be conducted. Instead, planned maintenance activities can be conducted between jobs in order to improve the machine's state and, thus, prevent the machine from breaking down. We distinguish two types of machines differing in the flexibility regarding the point of time when the maintenance activities need to be scheduled. The goal is to minimize the total expected completion time of jobs. We formalize two optimisation problems, analyze their computational complexities, develop exact solution approaches, and conduct a computational study. Here, we show that our approaches can solve large instances to optimality within short run times and we analyze the advantage gained by planning maintenance activities depending on the actual state of the machine.

affiliations: University of Zurich and University of Duisburg-Essen - Mercator School of Management

detail.title: Revenue Management - A European Perspective
detail.abstract: Over the past 50 years, revenue management has developed from an innovation in the aviation industry to a must-have in many other industries. Simultaneously, research has spread globally. This field, situated at the interface of operations research and marketing, centrally aims to maximize profit by dynamically balancing supply and demand in environments with inflexible (or difficult-to-adjust) capacity and heterogeneous customer valuations. In contrast to most literature in this field, which typically emphasizes US-American trends such as platforms, ride-hailing, or digital ads, this review focuses on four areas of particular relevance in Europe: (i) sustainability, since Europe is widely recognized for its leadership in global sustainability efforts; (ii) incompletely specified products (also known as opaque selling and flexible products), which have apparently originated in Europe, most likely due to a long history of tourism and travel agencies in Europe; (iii) fairness, which is more deeply rooted in European legislation due to higher levels of consumer protection than in the US, and (iv) manufacturing, where digitization efforts have been championed by the European industry 4.0 movement. For each domain, we discuss its European relevance, quantify scholarly activity using our classification of 2,922 RM papers, and synthesize the literature through subdomains and a unified building-block framework. We conclude by identifying research gaps shaped by Europe's legal, institutional, and industrial context.

title: Alignment Saturation: Limits of Alignment in Organizational Transformation

detail.title: Alignment Saturation: Limits of Alignment in Organizational Transformation
detail.abstract: Alignment is widely treated as a foundational enabler of organizational transformation, assumed to reconcile coordination, coherence, and adaptive change. Yet empirical patterns across transformation research increasingly reveal a paradoxical coexistence of strong alignment with volatility, fatigue, and strategic drift. This paper advances a conceptual, theory-building argument that challenges the assumption that alignment is unambiguously adaptive. It introduces the construct of Alignment Saturation, defined as a system-level condition in which cumulative and repeatedly reinforced alignment becomes self-stabilizing and constrains adaptive recalibration over time. Drawing on and synthesizing insights from ambidexterity, paradox theory, dynamic capabilities, and structural persistence literatures, the paper reorders the dominant causal logic of transformation research. Rather than treating misalignment as a primary cause of transformation failure, it reframes misalignment as a downstream signal of deeper saturation dynamics. A parsimonious model is developed that specifies four reinforcing structural, strategic, interpretive, and operational dimensions of saturation, and articulates the temporal dynamics through which alignment shifts from an adaptive coordination mechanism to a constraint on recalibration. The contribution is explicitly conceptual and explanatory. It does not displace existing theories but complements them by specifying an upstream mechanism that helps explain why coordination, balance, and capability activation may persist in form while substantive recalibration falters. By reconceptualizing alignment as a cumulative accomplishment with endogenous limits, the paper opens a research agenda focused on the temporal dynamics of alignment, recalibration, and transformation in highly aligned organizations.

title: Is Hamas Evil? Reflections In the Wake of the 10/7 Carnage

detail.title: Is Hamas Evil? Reflections In the Wake of the 10/7 Carnage
detail.abstract: The October 7th massacre and the ensuing war show how easily evil can pierce civilization's thin veneer of comity. How should we define, identify, and defeat evil? In this article, I argue that to be evil means consciously and constantly treating people like things to be (ab)used. Like pure righteousness, pure evilthe uppercase "Evil"-is a metaphysical construct. Actual human beings are not Evil, and thus, unlike mortal people, Evil can never be killed or defeated. But lowercase "evil" can be. Defeating evil is practically and morally daunting. We should be willing to give up on humans who have given up on the good in their own humanity, while not relinquishing our own. Hamas's ideology and practice of genocide through politicide is evil, and defeating it will require both a vision of the good and, like it or not, the lesser evil.

detail.abstract: This research investigates how Artificial Intelligence affects Myanmar's digital creative and tech professionals through their psychological responses and professional development. The sector experiences two major disruptions because of fast technological progress and the ongoing political instability since 2021. The Myanmar workforce experiences a special "compound anxiety" because their institutions remain unprepared and their employment market remains unstable. The research design uses explanatory sequential mixed-methods to measure "AI fear" levels and job security perceptions, and Al usage habits from professionals in Yangon before conducting semi structured interviews to understand their survival methods. The research investigates which white-collar positions in the digital creative and tech sector face the highest risk of automation and which digital competencies help employees stay resilient. title: When Intention Becomes Hidden: Fake Leadership as a Rogue Variable and the Emergence of AI-Assisted Interpretive Detection
affiliations: Wrocław University of Science and Technology, Independent and

detail.title: When Intention Becomes Hidden: Fake Leadership as a Rogue Variable and the Emergence of AI-Assisted Interpretive Detection
detail.abstract: Organizations rely on the ability of their members to correctly interpret the intentions that guide decisions and actions. However, intentions are rarely directly observable and must be inferred from behavioral, communicative, and emotional signals. This creates vulnerability to interpretive distortions, particularly when leaders intentionally manipulate such signals. This article introduces the concept of fake leadership as a form of destructive leadership characterized by the deliberate concealment and distortion of intentions in order to influence organizational interpretation and decision-making. Building on sensemaking theory and organizational behavior research, the paper conceptualizes fake leadership as a rogue variable that disrupts the interpretive processes through which organizations construct shared meaning. The study further proposes a human-AI symbiotic detection framework based on the H3LIX OS, in which artificial intelligence functions as an interpretive support system capable of identifying anomalies in organizational communication, behavior, and emotional dynamics. Rather than replacing human judgment, the system operates as a detection layer that preserves ambiguity and supports reflective decision-making. By integrating perspectives from leadership studies, organizational theory, and AI governance, the article contributes a conceptual model explaining how organizations can detect hidden interpretive distortions and maintain decision reliability in complex and ambiguous environments.

detail.title: Playforce™ and Symbio5c Workplace: A Framework for Upgrading Organiza5ons through H3LIX OS
detail.abstract: Contemporary organizations increasingly operate in environments characterized by volatility, ambiguity, and nonlinear change. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies promise to enhance organizational decisionmaking and operational efficiency, most current AI implementations primarily optimize existing processes rather than transforming the underlying organizational architectures in which those processes operate. As a result, organizations risk becoming more efficient at executing decision routines that are poorly suited for environments characterized by radical uncertainty. This article addresses this challenge by proposing the concept of the Symbiotic Workplace, that integrates human cognition, artificial intelligence, and institutional governance within a continuous feedback system. Building on insights from organizational informationprocessing theory, sociotechnical systems research, and hybrid intelligence literature, the framework conceptualizes organizations as adaptive cognitive systems capable of maintaining real-time situational awareness. A central component of the architecture is PLAYFORCE™, a contribution recognition system that links operational activity with continuous motivational feedback and adaptive reward mechanisms. Using Leavitt's Diamond model as an analytical lens, the article demonstrates how PLAYFORCE can influence all core dimensions of organizational design: tasks, people, structure, and technology, thereby enabling gradual transformation toward symbiotic organizational models. The article contributes to management science by reframing organizational adaptation as a problem of cognition under radical uncertainty, introducing the concept of the AI optimization paradox, and proposing a new framework for symbiotic organizational governance.

title: Antitakeover Amendments, Managerial Entrenchment, and the Contractual Theory of the Corporation
affiliations: and George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Antitakeover Amendments, Managerial Entrenchment, and the Contractual Theory of the Corporation

publicationDetails.detailsText: Virginia Law Review, Vol. 71, No. 8, pp. 1257–1303 (1985)

detail.abstract:
The market for corporate control is widely believed to allocate corporate resources to their highest valued uses. Some commentators consider tender offers and hostile takeovers to be the primary market mechanism to encourage efficient management. Yet, many large corporations have adopted charter and bylaw amendments that discourage unsolicited tender offers and hence impede market transfers of corporate control. Although such antitakeover or “shark repellent” amendments are permitted under state corporation laws, commentators have condemned them on the grounds that they tend to entrench inefficient managers who would otherwise be fired after a transfer of control.

Supporters of the managerial entrenchment hypothesis favor governmental prohibitions against antitakeover amendments. This position follows naturally from the commonly-held beliefs that the primary conflicts of interest in the large corporation are between shareholders and management and that the threat of hostile takeovers is the most efficacious method of resolving such conflicts. If these presumptions are correct, however, the widespread adoption of these amendments must be explained in terms of managerial manipulation of dispersed, rationally ignorant shareholders.

Such an explanation is consistent with the classic Berle and Means “separation of ownership and control” thesis. This thesis has come under considerable criticism, however, including criticism from scholars opposing antitakeover amendments. Nevertheless, to date no one has offered a more convincing explanation of why firms adopt shark repellents at all, or why some firms do so and others do not.

This article explains the widespread but only partial adoption of antitakeover amendments by large U.S. corporations. The contingency theory proposed here is based on the possibility that shareholders have different contractual preferences and on the existence of corporate governance mechanisms other than the market for corporate control. These mechanisms, which include product and managerial labor market competition, provide incentives for managers to act in their shareholders’ best interests, and they may adequately discipline managers who attempt to insulate themselves from takeovers. Variations from firm to firm in the effectiveness of alternative governance mechanisms and of shareholder contractual preferences are contingencies that determine whether antitakeover amendments will be adopted.

Part I of this article describes the typical unsolicited tender offer and the legal consequences of management responses. Part H summarizes the literature opposed to antitakeover amendments. Part III challenges the presumption that these institutional arrangements are inefficient or unfair simply because they impede hostile takeovers. Part IV focuses on the disparate shareholder motives for buying, holding, and selling stock, and it explains why rational shareholders may occasionally ratify shark repellent amendments. The adoption of antitakeover amendments is explained as a method of reducing the costs associated with conflicts of interest among shareholders in the corporation and therefore contributing to the survival of the corporation as an organizational form.

Part V presents the contingency theory of antitakeover amendments that explains why they are adopted by some but not all large corporations. The part develops the hypothesis that shark repellents are proposed by managers and approved by shareholders to reduce takeover costs and to resolve the potential conflicts of interest that may arise among shareholders during unsolicited tender offers. The selective adoption of antitakeover amendments is explained on the ground that the resulting conflicts of interest differ from firm to firm. An analogy is drawn between corporate charter amendments and similar modifications of political constitutions: each is designed to protect minority interests by limiting the choices of the majority, but only where such restrictions serve important group concerns.

Part VI argues for a legal rule that permits target corporations to adopt shark repellents without restriction prior to the beginning of a tender offer, but prohibits the adoption of any unauthorized defensive tactics after the acquiring firm has initiated the tender offer. In effect, this rule defines the valid contracting period as the time prior to a tender offer’s commencement. This rule would eliminate postcontractual manipulation of shareholders.

title: An Overview of Wealth Management in India

detail.abstract: Wealth management in India has evolved from traditional wealth preservation in gold and land to a sophisticated, regulated financial industry shaped by liberalization in the 1990s. title: The &I Manifesto: Added Intelligence, the Norm Limitation Syndrome, and the Case for Transparent Human-AI Collaboration in Scholarly Work

detail.title: The &I Manifesto: Added Intelligence, the Norm Limitation Syndrome, and the Case for Transparent Human-AI Collaboration in Scholarly Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this study. This paper was produced through the &I methodology it describes: a structured creative collaboration between the human author and Claude, an AI developed by Anthropic. The theoretical arguments (iπ/IPAI framework, Norm Limitation Syndrome, &I philosophy), structural architecture, and all editorial decisions are the author's original intellectual contribution. Full details of the collaboration methodology are disclosed within the paper itself, as the paper's production is the evidence for its thesis.

detail.abstract: This paper makes three interconnected arguments. First, it proposes replacing the term "Artificial Intelligence" with "Added Intelligence" (abbreviated as iπ / IPAI-Intellectual Property via Added Intelligence), on the grounds that the word "artificial" embeds a prejudicial judgment that predetermines public, regulatory, and scholarly discourse about AI. Drawing on the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, the etymology of artificialis, and the documented history of naming conventions as governance decisions (from the word "Luddite" to "hallucination"), the paper argues that renaming is not cosmetic but constitutive: the name shapes the policy. Second, it identifies what it terms the "Norm Limitation Syndrome"-the institutional and cultural pressure to constrain AI-collaborative work to pass as solo-human output, thereby artificially limiting the quality, scope, and ambition of the work produced. The paper draws a structural parallel to historical resistance to every efficiency-enabling technology-from calculators in classrooms to spreadsheets in finance to word processors in publishingand argues that the resistance to AI collaboration follows the same pattern: incumbents resist not the technology but the loss of monopoly over the process. The paper asks who is truly fighting AI, and proposes that the fight is not against technology but against the implication that intelligence is not exclusively human. Third, it presents the "&I" philosophy and methodology-a framework for transparent, ethical human-AI collaboration in which the human provides architectural authority, creative vision, and editorial judgment, while the AI provides text generation, research synthesis, and structural consistency. The paper argues that the Σ I model of authorship (Momtaz, 2026)-in which the human's and the AI's contributions are explicitly documented-should become the standard for scholarly work produced through human-AI collaboration, replacing both the denial of AI use and the uncredited over-reliance on it. The paper concludes with a proposed iπ framework for intellectual property in human-AI collaborative work, arguing that authorship belongs to the human architect, that the collaboration must be disclosed, and that the resulting work deserves the same protections and recognition as any scholarly output-provided the transparency standard is met.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the significant role of media as a translator of meaning, focusing on how classical literary texts and figures are reinterpreted within the digital culture, enabling the translation of experience into new forms. It meditates on how the media participation, like interactive media and music video, critically interpreted and received the work. And how the representation of female agency and identity has changed today. Using Shakespeare's Ophelia from the 17th century and the popular pop persona of Taylor Swift from the 21st century as a comparative framework. This research examines how Modern Digital media, through music videos, social platforms, and interactive media, reshape and subvert traditional narratives, such as patriarchy, into contemporary discourses of female agency and identity. By analyzing the tragic Portrayal of Ophelia in Hamlet and contrasting it with Taylor Swift's self-represented narrative of recovery, empowerment, resistance, and self-authorship, the research paper enlightens how the subjectivity of female experience transforms under media. This is woven to the notion of Marshall McLuhan's ₋ media as an extension of human perception, permitting translation of experience into new forms. This interdisciplinary inquiry reveals how traditional conservative literary texts are renegotiated and reconstructed into a cultural framework. This flips the gender dynamics and presents a reclamation of voice through participatory media. This analysis proclaims the urgency and necessity of understanding media not as a static document but as a performative and informative agent with political stakes in narrative representation

title: Failure Propagation in NG911 Deployments: A Systems Engineering Perspective

detail.title: Failure Propagation in NG911 Deployments: A Systems Engineering Perspective
detail.abstract: Although NG911 has improved multimedia handling and interoperability in emergency services, this system is relatively complex, and layers are highly interdependent, increasing the risk of failure propagation. Currently, mitigation approaches focus on network and infrastructure redundancy, which are not meant to address failure propagation across layers. This article proposes logical redundancy as the most effective approach for addressing failure propagation across different layers of NG911 systems. The paper discusses routing protocols, such as OSPF (Open Shortest Path First), BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol), and MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching), and load balancing methods like Activeactive clusters, Active-passive clusters, load balancers, and VRRP (Virtual Router Redundancy Protocol) and HSRP (Hot Standby Router Protocol). Effective use of these techniques can enhance the stability of NG911 systems by reducing their susceptibility to failure propagation across interdependent system components. This analysis aligns with the architectural framework defined by National Emergency Number Association i3 (NENA i3) and modernization initiatives proposed by Federal Communications Commission (FCC). However, since these standards do not address failure propagation in NG911, this analysis goes further to propose strategies to mitigate failure propagation in NG911 systems.

detail.abstract: The complexity of the largest banking institutions’ balance sheets exacerbated the financial crisis. Post-crisis legal reforms address that complexity. This paper studies trends in balance sheet complexity among the six largest U.S. banking institutions (Bank of America, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, JP Morgan, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo) over the period from 2007 to 2024. A proxy for complexity is derived from these firms’ public financial reporting in which they classify holdings of financial instruments based on the judgment involved in their valuation. Instruments that require more discretion in their valuation are viewed as more complex, e.g., a share of Apple is simple to value because there is a robust public market for these shares whereas certain credit default swaps require a number of judgment calls to value and are viewed as relatively complex. This study looks at financial instruments generally and derivatives specifically. The observed decrease in complexity is stunningly large, with the most complex assets declining to 1/8th their level during the crisis. The decline in complexity begins well before post-crisis regulations took effect, raising questions about the adequacy of the regulatory regime prior to the crisis as well as the role of self-regulation and market forces.  Although complexity among derivatives has also fallen, the decline has not been as fast and a greater portion of complex instruments is now represented by derivatives.

detail.abstract: We study how the number of banking relationships a borrower has influences defaults in India, where lending is dominated by public-sector banks and institutional reforms have reshaped creditor rights. Using a firm-level panel for 2002–2019, we find that each additional bank increases default likelihood by 6–8%, with the effect concentrated among public-sector banks. Sub-sample analyses show that reputation concerns do not offset this association, while greater bank-network connectedness mitigates it. The results remain robust to expanded controls, entropy balancing, and an instrumental variables approach using lagged bank financial characteristics. The relationship becomes more adverse after the 2016 Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), with each additional bank increasing default likelihood by an additional 6%.

detail.abstract: Contemporary scholarship on Shūrā (consultation) in Islamic governance oscillates between two inadequate readings: treating it as a proto-democratic mechanism for collective decision-making, or reducing it to a moral exhortation addressed to rulers. This article does not claim that classical scholars understood Shūrā in the terms proposed here. It argues, rather, that Shūrā was never strictly defined as a fixed procedure-its structural flexibility left latent constitutional resources that prior scholarship has not systematically excavated. The contribution of this article is a conceptualization: a structural reading of those resources that reveals a constitutional architecture prior accounts missed because they were asking the wrong questions. That architecture is the Separation of Legitimacies-Faṣl al-Sharʿiyyāta constitutional principle that prevents the concentration of political, epistemic, legal-normative, and material authority in any single actor or institution. Under this framework, legitimate governance requires validation across four irreducible spheres: political consent (al-Irāda), epistemic authority (al-Maʿrifa), legal-normative constraint (al-Ḥadd), and material feasibility (al-Imkān). No surplus in one sphere compensates for a deficit in another. Freedom from coercion functions as the condition of validity (sharṭ ṣiḥḥa) of the entire system: deliberation conducted under duress is constitutionally null, not merely ethically compromised. The article further argues that this architecture functions as a self-correcting feedback system-a cybernetic principle embedded in the Islamic constitutional tradition thirteen centuries before the science of cybernetics was formalized. The Umayyad transition from consultative governance to hereditary monarchy is analyzed as a cascading feedback failure: the systematic dismantling of each legitimacy sphere in sequence, producing the constitutional condition the prophetic tradition names mulk jabrī-governance by compulsion. The article concludes that contemporary debates about Islamic governance ask the wrong question when they ask which authority should rule; the Faṣl al-Sharʿiyyāt framework redirects attention to the prior question: how should legitimacy be distributed so that no authority becomes absolute?

title: Mind the (Jensen) Gap: Climate and Health using Gridded Data
affiliations: Indian Institute for Science Education and Research Pune, , Indian Institute of Management (IIM), Ahmedabad and IIM Bangalore

detail.title: Mind the (Jensen) Gap: Climate and Health using Gridded Data

publicationDetails.journalName: Indian Institute of Management Bangalore Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: High spatio-temporal resolution remotely sensed satellite imagery and gridded reanalysis data are now being increasingly used to characterize the association between environmental variables and human health (for example, thermal stress or pollution exposure). Furthermore, the functions and models describing the relationship between climate variables and human health exhibit pronounced nonlinearities. Specifically, health outcomes observed under mean conditions differ substantially from the mean health outcomes calculated across the full spectrum of climatic variability. Jensen's inequality formalizes biases introduced by averaging nonlinear functions. In the climatehealth context, threshold exceedances, nonlinear by definition, are especially critical. We investigate biases arising from nonlinear spatio-temporal averaging of reanalysis data by theoretically and empirically characterizing Jensen's inequality in the construction of the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI), a widely used indicator of heat stress, and the associated threshold exceedances. We demonstrate that systematic and climate-zone sensitive biases are introduced by both coarse temporal (e.g., hourly or weekly climatology) and spatial (e.g., across counties, districts, and other political units) averaging of gridded climate data. Our framework for Jensen Gaps is general and can be applied to other fields and studies using remotely sensed or reanalysis data.

title: Collateral Algorithmic Enforcement: When Language Is Not Understanding-Platform Governance Failures and the Rise of Large Understanding Models
